items.descriptionOriginal: “Nobody can love that face.” Today, she’s a finalist in Miss India Uttar Pradesh. ❤️ Born with a port-wine stain on her face, she grew up facing stares, cruel comments and bullying. At school, children told her she was weird and refused to sit with her. The hurt followed her everywhere. She began skipping school, avoiding photographs and hiding from people. There was a time when she couldn't even look at herself in the mirror. Then her sister encouraged her to do something that terrified her: stand in front of a camera. With her sister by her side, she slowly began creating content and exploring modelling. Even when online trolls called her ugly, she stopped trying to fit into someone else's definition of beauty. The girl who once avoided cameras is now a Miss India Uttar Pradesh finalist and has won the People's Choice Award. Today, people reach out to tell her that her journey has helped them embrace themselves. She isn't celebrated because she overcame a visible difference. She's celebrated because she refused to let prejudice decide how much space she deserved to take up. Her face was never something to be ashamed of. And now, she wants others to know that they never have to hide theirs either. ❤️ #MissIndiaUttarPradesh #PortWineStain #BirthmarkAwareness #SelfLove #BodyPositivity #BeautyBeyondAppearance #StopBullying #Confidence #PageantJourney #BreakingStereotypes #Acceptance #WomenWhoInspire #RealBeauty #InspiringStories #TheBetterIndia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

Την έρευνα, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο Psychology and Aging , παρουσιάζει η αναλύτρια συμπεριφοράς, Δρ. Wendy L. Patrick στο Psychology Today . Τι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Το αίσθημα ότι μπορούμε να επηρεάσουμε την καθημερινότητά μας φαίνεται να έχει ιδιαίτερη σημασία για την ευτυχία όσο μεγαλώνουμε. Νέα μελέτη συνδέει την αίσθηση ελέγχου με μικρότερη συναισθηματική επιβάρυνση από τις αλλαγές που αποδίδουμε στην ηλικία. Την έρευνα, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο Psychology and Aging , παρουσιάζει η αναλύτρια συμπεριφοράς, Δρ. Wendy L. Patrick στο Psychology Today . Τι έδειξαν οι καθημερινές καταγραφές Στη μελέτη συμμετείχαν 268 ενήλικες ηλικίας 50 έως 91 ετών , οι οποίοι κρατούσαν ημερολόγιο για 14 ημέρες. Κατέγραφαν τις αλλαγές που αντιλαμβάνονταν ως απώλειες ή οφέλη της ηλικίας, πόσο ευτυχισμένοι αισθάνονταν και σε ποιον βαθμό θεωρούσαν ότι μπορούσαν να επηρεάσουν τη ζωή τους. Τις ημέρες που αναγνώριζαν περισσότερες απώλειες ή λιγότερα οφέλη από το πέρασμα του χρόνου, ανέφεραν χαμηλότερα επίπεδα ευτυχίας . Η σύνδεση αυτή ήταν εντονότερη όταν ένιωθαν ότι είχαν μικρότερο έλεγχο στην καθημερινότητά τους. Τι σημαίνει να αισθανόμαστε ότι έχουμε επιλογές Η αίσθηση ελέγχου αφορά την πεποίθηση ότι οι πράξεις και οι αποφάσεις μας μπορούν να επηρεάσουν όσα συμβαίνουν στη ζωή μας. Όπως εξηγεί η Δρ. Patrick, αυτή η αντίληψη μπορεί να κινητοποιεί την ενεργή αντιμετώπιση των δυσκολιών και την προσαρμογή στις αλλαγές της ηλικίας. Στο άρθρο της αναδεικνύει και έναν πιθανό φαύλο κύκλο: ο φόβος ενός τραυματισμού μπορεί να οδηγήσει σε περιορισμό της σωματικής δραστηριότητας , στερώντας ευκαιρίες διατήρησης της φυσικής κατάστασης. Αντίστοιχα, η απομάκρυνση από ευχάριστες ασχολίες μπορεί να περιορίσει τις πηγές καθημερινής ικανοποίησης. Χώρος και για όσα κερδίζουμε μεγαλώνοντας Η Δρ. Patrick στρέφει την προσοχή και στις θετικές πλευρές της ηλικίας , όπως η εμπειρία, η υπομονή και η μεγαλύτερη εκτίμηση των σχέσεων. Η αναγνώρισή τους μπορεί να διευρύνει την εικόνα που έχουμε για τον εαυτό μας πέρα από τις δυσκολίες και τους περιορισμούς. Οι ερευνητές προτείνουν να εξεταστεί η ενίσχυση της αίσθησης ελέγχου , μαζί με μια θετικότερη αντίληψη για τη γήρανση, στον σχεδιασμό παρεμβάσεων υποστήριξης των μεγαλύτερων ενηλίκων. Παρόλο που τα ευρήματα καταγράφουν συσχετίσεις σε διάστημα δύο εβδομάδων, χωρίς να αποδεικνύουν σχέση αιτίας και αποτελέσματος, αναδεικνύουν τη σημασία του να αισθάνεται κανείς ότι εξακολουθεί να έχει λόγο στις επιλογές της ζωής του. items.title: Η δεξιότητα των παιδιών που δημιουργεί ευτυχισμένους ενήλικες – Τι έδειξε έρευνα για το «μάθημα της χελώνας»
items.titleOriginal: Η δεξιότητα των παιδιών που δημιουργεί ευτυχισμένους ενήλικες – Τι έδειξε έρευνα για το «μάθημα της χελώνας»
items.description: Μια βαθιά ανάσα, μια μικρή παύση και λίγες λέξεις για όσα νιώθουμε. Μπορεί μια τόσο απλή άσκηση στην τρυφερή ηλικία των 4 ετών να επηρεάζει την ψυχική μας υγεία σχεδόν 20 χρόνια αργότερα; Νέα μελέτη του Πανεπιστημίου Penn State, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο American Psychologist , δείχνει πώς η εκμάθηση συναισθηματικών και κοινωνικών δεξιοτήτων στην προσχολική ηλικία συνδέεται με μειωμένα συμπτώματα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Μια βαθιά ανάσα, μια μικρή παύση και λίγες λέξεις για όσα νιώθουμε. Μπορεί μια τόσο απλή άσκηση στην τρυφερή ηλικία των 4 ετών να επηρεάζει την ψυχική μας υγεία σχεδόν 20 χρόνια αργότερα; Νέα μελέτη του Πανεπιστημίου Penn State, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο American Psychologist , δείχνει πώς η εκμάθηση συναισθηματικών και κοινωνικών δεξιοτήτων στην προσχολική ηλικία συνδέεται με μειωμένα συμπτώματα κατάθλιψης, μοναξιάς και μεγαλύτερη ικανοποίηση από τη ζωή. Οι επιστήμονες παρακολούθησαν 356 παιδιά από το νηπιαγωγείο έως τα 21-22 τους χρόνια, αναζητώντας τα μακροπρόθεσμα οφέλη μιας εκπαιδευτικής παρέμβασης. Το «μάθημα της χελώνας» Η έρευνα ξεκίνησε το 2003-2004, σε 44 τάξεις του αμερικανικού προγράμματος Head Start, που απευθύνεται κυρίως σε οικογένειες χαμηλού εισοδήματος, στην Πενσιλβάνια. Οι τάξεις χωρίστηκαν τυχαία σε δύο ομάδες: Η μία ακολούθησε το συνηθισμένο πρόγραμμα, ενώ η άλλη συμμετείχε στο εμπλουτισμένο πρόγραμμα REDI, με δραστηριότητες συναισθηματικής αγωγής και διαδραστικής ανάγνωσης . Μέσα από ιστορίες, κουκλοθέατρο και παιχνίδια ρόλων, τα παιδιά μάθαιναν να αναγνωρίζουν τα συναισθήματά τους, να διαχειρίζονται την απογοήτευση , να λύνουν διαφωνίες και να δείχνουν ενσυναίσθηση . Χαρακτηριστική ήταν η τεχνική «κάνω τη χελώνα»: Σταματώ πριν αντιδράσω, παίρνω μια βαθιά ανάσα και προσπαθώ να εξηγήσω τι με ενοχλεί και πώς αισθάνομαι. Οι εκπαιδευτικοί ενίσχυαν καθημερινά αυτές τις δεξιότητες, ενώ οι γονείς λάμβαναν υλικό για να συνεχίζουν την εξάσκηση στο σπίτι. Τι άλλαξε 20 χρόνια αργότερα Στην ηλικία των 21-22 ετών, οι ερευνητές συγκέντρωσαν στοιχεία από 263 συμμετέχοντες, περίπου το 74% του αρχικού δείγματος. Μέσα από τηλεφωνικές συνεντεύξεις αξιολόγησαν 11 δείκτες ψυχικής υγείας , κοινωνικών σχέσεων και ποιότητας ζωής. Όσοι είχαν παρακολουθήσει το πρόγραμμα REDI παρουσίασαν καλύτερα αποτελέσματα σε 7 δείκτες: Λιγότερα προβλήματα συμπεριφοράς και συμπτώματα κατάθλιψης Μειωμένη αίσθηση μοναξιάς Μεγαλύτερη ενσυναίσθηση Ισχυρότερη συναισθηματική υποστήριξη Περισσότερες ημέρες καλής υγείας Υψηλότερη ικανοποίηση από τη ζωή Είχαν, επίσης, μεγαλύτερη πιθανότητα να ανήκουν στην ομάδα με την υψηλότερη συνολική ευημερία. Οι διαφορές ήταν μικρές έως μέτριες, αλλά αξιοσημείωτες, δεδομένου ότι είχαν περάσει σχεδόν δύο δεκαετίες. Ποια παιδιά ωφελήθηκαν περισσότερο Οι επιστήμονες συνυπολόγισαν και τις δυσκολίες που είχαν αντιμετωπίσει οι συμμετέχοντες ως παιδιά, όπως έκθεση σε βία, αυστηρές τιμωρίες, οικογενειακή αστάθεια ή κατάθλιψη γονέα. Οι εμπειρίες αυτές συνδέθηκαν με περισσότερα προβλήματα συμπεριφοράς, υπερκινητικότητα , συμπτώματα κατάθλιψης και χαμηλότερη ικανοποίηση από τη ζωή. Ωστόσο, τα παιδιά που είχαν βιώσει περισσότερες αντιξοότητες φάνηκε να ωφελούνται περισσότερο από το πρόγραμμα ως προς την ενσυναίσθηση και την κοινωνικότητα . Στους άλλους 9 δείκτες δε διαπιστώθηκε αντίστοιχη διαφοροποίηση. Οφέλη με διάρκεια στον χρόνο Προηγούμενες αξιολογήσεις είχαν δείξει ότι τα αρχικά οφέλη του REDI στη γλώσσα εξασθένησαν ήδη από τις πρώτες τάξεις του δημοτικού. Αντίθετα, τα κοινωνικά και συναισθηματικά οφέλη παρέμειναν ορατά έως την εφηβεία και, όπως δείχνουν τα νέα δεδομένα, στην πρώιμη ενήλικη ζωή. Μια πιθανή εξήγηση είναι ότι τα παιδιά που μαθαίνουν να διαχειρίζονται τα συναισθήματά τους δημιουργούν καλύτερες σχέσεις με συμμαθητές και εκπαιδευτικούς. Αυτές οι εμπειρίες μπορούν, σταδιακά, να ενισχύσουν την κοινωνική προσαρμογή και την ψυχική ανθεκτικότητα . Οι ερευνητές διευκρινίζουν, ωστόσο, ότι η μελέτη έχει περιορισμούς: Βασίστηκε σε αυτοαναφορές συμμετεχόντων από τρεις συγκεκριμένες περιοχές. Παρά τις επιφυλάξεις, ωστόσο, το μήνυμα είναι ουσιαστικό: Η προσχολική εκπαίδευση δεν αφορά μόνο σε γράμματα και αριθμούς. Το να μάθει ένα παιδί να αναγνωρίζει όσα νιώθει, να ηρεμεί και να συνεργάζεται μπορεί να αποτελέσει πολύτιμο εφόδιο για τη ζωή του. Διαβάστε επίσης Τι εννοεί πραγματικά το παιδί όταν σας λέει «Είσαι η χειρότερη μαμά στον κόσμο» Οι έφηβοι είναι πολύ θυμωμένοι – Πώς να διαχειριστούν οι γονείς την εφηβική οργή 6 σημάδια ότι μεγαλώσατε με ναρκισσιστή γονέα – Τι αποκαλύπτουν οι ψυχολόγοι

items.titleOriginal: Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there’s a surprising catch
items.description: Μια τεράστια μελέτη σε σχεδόν 486.000 ενήλικες διαπίστωσε ότι η τακτική κατανάλωση τσαγιού συσχετίστηκε με 11% χαμηλότερο κίνδυνο καρδιακών και αιμοφόρων αγγείων. Ο χαμηλότερος κίνδυνος συνδέθηκε με την κατανάλωση περίπου έξι έως οκτώ φλιτζανιών την ημέρα, με το μαύρο τσάι να παρουσιάζει πιο σταθερά οφέλη από το πράσινο τσάι.
items.descriptionOriginal: A massive study of nearly 486,000 adults found that regularly drinking tea was associated with an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. The lowest risk was linked to drinking roughly six to eight cups per day, with black tea showing more consistent benefits than green tea.

items.descriptionOriginal: If you have standard human vision (even if assisted by glasses), chances are you’re adept at finding things, people, and paths to them. But if you have impaired vision, or none at all, countless tasks that are simple for fully sighted people become difficult, dangerous, or even impossible. Fortunately, plenty of new high-tech tools offer assistance, including robot guide dogs, a cane-bot (looking a bit like a small R2D2 with giant wheels), multiple types of smart glasses with descriptive audio, and even a haptic vest for blind dogs. items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. On the forested edges of Shillong, a camera trap recorded an animal that is rarely seen, even by those who study wildlife. Moving through the forest under the cover of darkness was a Chinese pangolin, a critically endangered mammal that has now been documented in the Wildlife Institute of India's (WII) study area in Meghalaya for the first time. The sighting is significant for more than the presence of a threatened species. Forests bordering urban areas may appear small compared with protected wilderness, but they can provide vital shelter for animals facing habitat loss and fragmentation. A rare visitor, recorded on camera The record emerged from WII's ongoing project, Assessment of Mammalian Assemblages in Meghalaya, which focuses on the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests along Shillong's urban edges . "This rare record comes from our ongoing project," the institute said, highlighting the first documentation of the Chinese pangolin within its Meghalaya study area. 🌿 A Milestone record on the Fringes of Shillong! 📸✨ Our camera traps have recorded the Critically Endangered Chinese Pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) for the very first time in our study area! 🛡️🐾 This rare record comes from our ongoing project "Assessment of Mammalian Assemblages in Meghalaya", focusing on the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests right on the urban edges of Shillong. These peri-urban city forests harbor a remarkably unique and diverse assemblage of wildlife. Alongside the Chinese pangolin, our cameras captured iconic species including the Large Indian Civet, Leopard Cat, Masked Palm Civet, Yellow-throated Marten, Indian Crested Porcupine, and Kalij Pheasant. 🌲 Why This Matters: Urban-adjacent and city-fringe forests are often overlooked, yet they act as critical ecological refuges for species threatened by habitat fragmentation and urban development. Finding a Critically Endangered specialist like the Chinese pangolin sharing space with a rich suite of carnivores and small mammals proves that these urban forest patches are invaluable biodiversity strongholds that must be strictly protected and preserved. 👥 @Himalayanwolf1 @lifeofawild @nishinath @supratikroy @meghalayaforest @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) October 20, 2026 The finding is particularly valuable because systematic information about the species' population and distribution across parts of Northeast India remains limited. Although the Chinese pangolin is known to occur in the region, there is little recent systematic data on its status and numbers. A camera-trap record does not, by itself, establish how many pangolins live in these forests or whether their population is stable. However, it confirms the species' presence in the study area and provides researchers with an important starting point for further monitoring. What makes the Chinese pangolin special? Pangolins are nocturnal insectivores, meaning they are active mainly at night and feed on insects. Their bodies are covered in overlapping scales, and when threatened, they curl into a tight ball, using their armoured exterior as protection. Yet these defences offer little protection against people. Pangolins are widely recognised as the most trafficked mammals in the world, making their survival a major conservation concern. Forests bordering urban areas may appear small compared with protected wilderness, but they can provide vital shelter for animals facing habitat loss and fragmentation. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust of India) Of the world's eight pangolin species, two are found in India: the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) and the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata). The Chinese pangolin is native to parts of the northern Indian subcontinent, northern Southeast Asia and southern China. In India, it occurs across northeastern states and northern West Bengal. Arunachal Pradesh is considered one of its strongholds. The species has been listed as Critically Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List since 2014, reflecting its severe risk of extinction in the wild. Can you tell the two Indian pangolins apart? Although both species are covered in protective scales, there are some distinguishing features: Scale size: The Chinese pangolin has smaller scales than the Indian pangolin. Tail: The Indian pangolin has a terminal scale on the underside of its tail. This scale is absent in the Chinese pangolin. Scale weight: The dry weight of scales from one Chinese pangolin is roughly 500–700 grams, compared with approximately 1.5–1.8 kg for an Indian pangolin. These differences can help distinguish the two species, though identifying an animal in the wild requires careful observation. More than a pangolin The Chinese pangolin was not the only animal recorded during WII's camera-trap study. The institute documented a range of other wildlife in the Riat Laban and Laitkor reserve forests, including the Large Indian Civet, Leopard Cat, Masked Palm Civet, Yellow-throated Marten, Indian Crested Porcupine and Kalij Pheasant. The presence of several mammals and birds also makes these sites valuable for understanding how different species use habitats close to human settlements. WII has described these peri-urban forests as harbouring a remarkably unique and diverse assemblage of wildlife. Why Shillong's forests matter Urban forests are often valued for their role in improving the quality of life for people, from providing green spaces to supporting local ecological processes. But their importance also lies in the wildlife they sustain, including species that may otherwise go unnoticed. "Finding a critically Endangered species like the Chinese pangolin sharing space with a rich suite of carnivores and small mammals proves that these urban forest patches are invaluable biodiversity strongholds that must be strictly protected and preserved," WII said. Protecting these forests will require recognising them as wildlife habitats, not simply undeveloped land around a city. Sources: 'Wildlife forensics helps cause of pangolins' : By Aswathi Pacha , Published on 8 May 2021 'Indigenous knowledge to track and save the Chinese pangolin' : By Nikhil Sreekandan, Published on 17 December 2025

Ήταν μια μικρή ομολογία, αλλά έφερε το βάρος μιας επιδημίας. Σε όλες τις πανεπιστημιουπόλεις των ΗΠΑ,…
items.descriptionOriginal: Somewhere between the gorges and botanic gardens of Cornell University's campus, a student on a guided nature walk looked up from hours of screen time and said something that stopped the walk leader cold: "This is the first time I've actually touched grass." It was a small confession, but it carried the weight of an epidemic. Across U.S. campuses, colleges are turning to "social prescribing" -- a practice borrowed from the UK where physicians write actual referrals, logged in electronic health records, for time in nature, art, movement, or community -- as a complement to counseling and medication for the surging mental health crisis among students. At Cornell, over 2,200 students received nature prescriptions last year, and 88 percent reported an improved mood. At Stanford, a dedicated care navigator connects students to pottery classes, dance workshops, and live performances -- and 80 percent of those who attended reported better mental health. What these programs are quietly surfacing is something older than any diagnosis: that belonging, beauty, and the sensory world are not luxuries but medicine. The student who finally touched grass wasn't being dramatic. She was describing a kind of return.

items.descriptionOriginal: For the children gathered around her, a patch of sand becomes their first writing book, and their fingers become pencils. At 85, Indira Amma from Kerala is introducing young learners to the world of letters through a traditional method passed down through generations. For the past decade, she has reportedly been teaching children Malayalam , Hindi, English, and mathematics using this humble approach. Instead of beginning with notebooks and pencils, she lets children trace letters in sand, helping them become familiar with the alphabet through touch and practice. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mom of Safachiiii 🤍 (@mom_of_safaachiiii) Her method draws on Kerala's tradition of Ezhuthiniruthu, a ceremony that marks a child's introduction to learning. Traditionally associated with Vijayadashami, the ritual involves guiding children to trace their first letters in rice or sand. The act symbolises the beginning of their educational journey. An endearing glimpse of this tradition shows Ashaatti Ammumma patiently teaching hindi alphabets to young children at the Temple of English School. As the children follow along, each letter becomes an opportunity to learn through practice, guided by her gentle approach. For young children, learning to recognise and write letters takes patience and repetition . Tracing them in sand offers an experiential way to understand their shapes, allowing little learners to practise each movement as they grow more confident. What makes this approach special is how it connects everyday learning with a tradition strongly rooted in Kerala's cultural heritage. At a time when classrooms are embracing digital tools, it is a reminder that learning need not always begin with a screen or expensive resources. Sometimes, all it takes is a handful of sand, someone willing to guide a child's hand , and the time to let them learn at their own pace. Through this practice, Indira Amma is helping keep a traditional way of learning alive while giving young children a meaningful start to their educational journeys.

items.descriptionOriginal: The silica gel packets you find in the pockets of your clothes after a shopping day or inside a box of new shoes come with a stern, scary warning : “Throw away. Do not eat.” But as long as you don’t eat them (or let small kids or pets get to them), you actually don’t need to throw them away. Instead, you can reuse the silica packets. They contain desiccant, a drying agent, used by manufacturers to help keep moisture from damaging clothing or electronics during shipping. They’re also found in some packaged foods since they help keep your favorite snack fresh. (One exception: the “Do Not Eat” packet in a bag of beef jerky is usually an oxygen absorber filled with iron powder, not silica gel, and it can’t be recharged.) It turns out these little packets aren’t just for one-time use. They actually can be dried out and used again and again with a few simple steps. If you think that sounds like a stretch, think again. These packets can be used a number of ways right inside your own home. A lesson in sustainability TikTok creator @trash.dates posted a series of videos in May and June 2026 explaining why you shouldn’t throw out those silica packets. They also showed off their impressive stash. In the video, they shared that the packets absorb moisture in the air and described how to make them reusable. By putting the packets in the sun to dry out, you can reuse them many times. Some are even color-coded to let you know when the packets are full of moisture and need to be dried out, and when they’re ready for use again. In this video, orange beads signify the packet is dry. When they turn green, they’re full of moisture. (Older blue-to-pink indicator beads can contain cobalt chloride, which is toxic , so keep those away from food.) There is one caveat the creator points out: the drying agent in the packet can irritate your eyes, nose, throat, or skin, so you’ll want to be careful not to handle a broken packet. As for the warning not to eat them, Poison Control says silica gel is non-toxic, but the packets are a choking hazard, so keep them away from small children and pets. The internet had hacks, too While some TikTok users had more questions than answers about how to use these silica packets (more on that below), others weighed in with their own hacks for reusing the product. “I put them in my car to prevent mold and prevent the fog condensation in the morning,” one user wrote. “A tip from a silversmith: these can also be put in your jewelry box to reduce moisture & keep your pieces from tarnishing!!! Especially sterling silver,” another added. “I use them for everything … if you live in a humid environment don’t forget to put them near your makeup powders,” said another user. “I toss these behind the books on my bookshelf to keep the pages from getting moldy,” added another user. More uses than you think The popularity of the first video and a comment section filled with people learning about this hack for the first time prompted trash.dates to make a follow-up. This one features a handful of ways to use these “forbidden packets.” Unfortunately, using rice to dry out your moisture-logged phone is a myth, and Apple warns that rice particles can actually damage an iPhone. Rice simply isn’t as effective a desiccant as silica gel. Apple’s advice for a wet iPhone is to unplug it, tap out excess liquid, and leave it somewhere dry with airflow for up to a day before charging. A few silica packets in a sealed bag with the phone may help, but for a laptop that took a coffee spill, powering it down and getting it checked matters more. The video also suggests using them to help seeds, spices, and food stay fresh longer. (As a precaution, use only intact, food-grade packets, never blue-to-pink indicator beads, and keep them from touching the food.) Storing foods with silica gel packets can help preserve freshness. Photo credit: Flickr . Practical practices Drying flowers with the beads (the creator specifies “beads only,” not the whole packet) also has a different result than hanging them to dry. According to the video, the silica packets help preserve the color of the flowers and prevent them from looking crunchy. Like some users mentioned on the previous video, the silica packets can also help keep your jewelry from oxidizing. They’re also great for keeping metal, like silverware or tools, from rusting. Have some funky-smelling sneakers, a gym bag, or sports equipment? Stick these babies in there. Camping gear in your garage? You guessed it: these will help keep your sleeping bag and tent dry and mold-free when you aren’t using them. Good for prevention For people who live in cold climates, silica packets can help reduce fog and condensation on the inside of your windshield. Those annoying winter drives just got a lot easier to navigate. They’re also great for preventing mold and mildew in household places like under sinks, in storage tote bins, and in the laundry room, according to the creator. You may also keep them with important documents to reduce moisture and mildew, though they can’t protect against leaks or floods. @trash.dates I truly didn’t expect so many of you to have already saved and found incredible use for silica gel! list compiled below! -saving wet electronics -storing seeds -keeping the inside of your car from fogging/FREEZING -drying flowers (beads only) -keeps jewelry from oxidizing -keeps food fresh longer -keeps books from molding -keeps silverware & other metal from RUSTING -fights funky bacteria in gym/sports bags -prevents mold in camping gear -keeping laundry rooms & under sinks dryer -keeping storage items from bad moisture buildup -fights moisture in any humid environment -keeps inside of shoes/skates/blades/boots fresher -keeps important documents safer -all around great to fight/prevent water damage -keeping products from clumping Did we forget anything?? Drop a comment below! PS: DO NOT ASK CHAT. Chat knows NOTHING of the human experience. #reduce #reuse #recycle #fyp #silicagel ♬ Reduce Reuse Recycle – Blake Rules & Netherfriends Don’t forget to recharge While using the silica packets to keep your prized possessions dry and tarnish-free is relatively simple, there’s one step you might not realize you need to do. Every so often, you’ll need to dry them out so they can absorb more moisture, a process trash.dates calls “recharging.” Even those who already save and reuse the packets didn’t know this. “I’ve been using them in my linen closet, but didn’t realize I needed to ‘recharge’ them in the sunlight, thank you!” said one user. One final video in this mini-series shows the two best ways to “recharge” a packet. First, you can let them dry in the sun as mentioned. Second, you can spread them out on a paper towel, add another paper towel on top of them, and place a regular plate on top of that to hold them in place. Then, pop them in the microwave for two-minute intervals until they are dry and ready to store. Check your packets first: some paper or fabric packets can melt or scorch in a microwave, so many sources recommend a low oven instead (around 200°F for two hours), and orange indicator beads should return to orange before you store them. @trash.dates Just a girl and her microwave #reuse #silicagel #sustainability #fyp ♬ Fresh Affiliate – DJ BAI “This is information I’m going to share with everyone at work tomorrow. thanks for using your brain and other people’s help to put this list together,” one user said. So, the next time you’re about to head to the garbage can with these silica packets in tow, don’t. Instead, save them up and use and reuse them to help cut down on moisture and its pesky effects around your home. This article originally appeared in June. It has been updated. The post Those silica gel packets are actually endlessly reusable, and so useful appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: When you find a true friend, it can be one of life’s greatest gifts. But not all friendships are created equal, and what defines “friendship” varies from person to person. Is a friend someone you enjoy hanging out with? Someone you can confide in? Someone who always has your back? What makes someone a friend has been a question people have pondered since ancient times, as evidenced by Aristotle’s musings on the subject in the fourth century B.C. The famous philosopher wrote that friendship doesn’t only differ in degree, but in type , stating that there are three distinct kinds of friends people can have. Did you know Aristotle thought friendship was more important than justice? Near the end of the Nicomachean Ethics, he writes, "When men are friends, they have no need of justice, but when they are just, they still need friendship." His point is simple. Laws exist because… pic.twitter.com/eC4lgBWuqS — Athenaeum Book Club (@athenaeumbc) July 6, 2026 Friendships of utility Some friendships are somewhat transactional in nature, where each person gets something useful out of the relationship. “Those who love each other for their utility do not love each other for themselves but in virtue of some good which they get from each other,” Aristotle wrote, saying that “friendship based on utility is for the commercially minded.” An example of a friendship of utility might be a friendship you have with your coworkers or business colleagues. You may genuinely like one another, but if one of you leaves the work environment, the friendship goes with it. Another example might be between a host and a guest who frequents an establishment regularly. “Now the useful is not permanent but is always changing,” Aristotle wrote. “Thus when the motive of the friendship is done away, the friendship is dissolved, inasmuch as it existed only for the ends in question. This kind of friendship seems to exist chiefly between old people (for at that age people pursue not the pleasant but the useful) and, of those who are in their prime or young, between those who pursue utility.” Friendships of pleasure Some friendships form because people like and enjoy something about one another. Maybe you have fun and laugh together. Perhaps you take pleasure in the same things like sports, art or music, and share that with one another. Or maybe you just find one another entertaining. This kind of friendship feels good, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that it will last. “It is not for their character that men love ready-witted people, but because they find them pleasant,” Aristotle wrote. Friendships of pleasure are based on more personal foundations than friendships of utility, but they still only go so far and so deep. “Those who love for the sake of pleasure do so for the sake of what is pleasant to themselves, and not in so far as the other is the person loved but in so far as he is useful or pleasant,” wrote Aristotle. Friendships of utility and pleasure are “only incidental,” he asserted, adding, “for it is not as being the man he is that the loved person is loved, but as providing some good or pleasure. Such friendships, then, are easily dissolved, if the parties do not remain like themselves; for if the one party is no longer pleasant or useful the other ceases to love him.” Friendships of the good “Perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good, and alike in virtue; for these wish well alike to each other qua good, and they are good themselves,” Aristotle wrote. (If you’re unfamiliar with the word “qua,” it means “in capacity of” or “as being.”) Friendships of the good are much less common than those of utility or pleasure, partially because they require two people who have some base level of similar virtue, and partially because they take time to build. “But it is natural that such friendships should be infrequent; for such men are rare,” Aristotle wrote. “Further, such friendship requires time and familiarity; as the proverb says, men cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’; nor can they admit each other to friendship or be friends till each has been found lovable and been trusted by each. Those who quickly show the marks of friendship to each other wish to be friends, but are not friends unless they both are lovable and know the fact; for a wish for friendship may arise quickly, but friendship does not.” Friendships of the good have the potential to make us better people , as they are based on character qualities that are mutually encouraged. These friendships tend to last a lifetime and are the kinds of friendships most people desire. They may also be getting harder to find: in 2021, 12% of U.S. adults said they had no close friends, up from 3% in 1990, according to the Survey Center on American Life, as reported by the American Psychological Association . How to build friendships of the good So, how do we go about finding such friends and creating and maintaining such friendships? First, don’t expect to have a ton of them. “One cannot be a friend to many people in the sense of having friendship of the perfect type with them, just as one cannot be in love with many people at once,” Aristotle wrote. Marisa Franco , author of Platonic: How the Science of Attachment Can Help You Make and Keep Friends, shared some tips for building real friendships in her book : Take initiative “We have to put ourselves out there and try. It’s a process of reaching out over and over again,” writes Franco. A woman speaks on the telephone. Photo credit: Canva It’s hard to make friends if you’re not connecting with people, so start there. Reach out to an old friend you haven’t talked to in a long time. Find groups to join that may have people who share your interests or values . Don’t wait for others to come to you or for friendship to drop in your lap. Be willing to be vulnerable and to receive vulnerability A big part of friendship is sharing our feelings, which includes our joys and hopes as well as our fears and frustrations. It’s hard to develop intimacy without some deep sharing, but we also have to be prepared to receive others’ vulnerability as well. “ Understanding and feeling attuned to others’ vulnerability is a key to developing and deepening friendships, and missing those cues can jeopardize them,” writes Franco. Be real Franco says letting people see our authentic selves is important, but that doesn’t mean letting it all hang out. Authenticity happens when “we aren’t triggered, when we can make intentional, rather than reactive, decisions about how we want to show up in the world,” she says. However, Franco also warns that it might take some time and discernment, and that it might be necessary to vet potential friends before showing them our full selves. It doesn’t have to be a hug, but showing affection helps solidify friendship. Photo credit: Canva “In a perfect world, we would all be loved in our most authentic form, but in the real world, privilege plays into whose authentic self is welcomed and whose is rejected,” she writes. And, of course, being vulnerable and authentic isn’t all that easy for many of us. It is, however, necessary. As Aristotle noted, this kind of friendship “requires time and familiarity,” and that’s not an easy thing to give. Show affection “The more you show affection, the more likely you are to not just make friends, but also deepen the friendships you already have,” writes Franco. Affection can be emotional, physical, or both, and different people may prefer to receive it in different ways. But letting people know you love them and care about the friendship is key. Practice generosity Being generous with our time, thoughts, and energy matters in friendship . Sometimes that may involve some sacrifice, though we also need to be careful not to sacrifice too much for too many people. Really, it’s just about making some selfless efforts. “For friendship to flourish, we need to know if we call a friend crying because we got fired from our job at the nuclear power plant, they won’t text back, ‘I am currently unavailable,'” Franco writes. And, of course, if you really want an Aristotelian friendship of the good, you can work on your own character as well, honing the virtues you will bring to that “perfect” friendship when you find it. Which type are you actually building? Most of us have plenty of utility friendships and a handful of pleasure friendships, and there’s nothing wrong with either. They serve real purposes and make life easier and more enjoyable. But Aristotle’s point is that the third kind is rare, and it’s the one most people actually want. The good news is that it’s not a matter of luck: one study Franco cites found that people who believed friendship happens by luck were lonelier five years later, while those who saw it as taking effort were less lonely. It’s a matter of time, intention, and being the kind of person someone else would want a friendship of the good with. That part, at least, is entirely within your control. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Aristotle said there are 3 different types of friendship. One of them makes us better people. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Do you tend to experience jealousy, have difficulty trusting people, or resist emotional intimacy out of fear? While genetics can play a role in qualities like these presenting themselves, they may also be explained by attachment theory: the idea that our earliest relationships influence how we’ll connect with people later in life. “As children, we build our understanding of relationships based on our caregivers,” Jennifer Rolnick , a licensed clinical psychologist and co-owner of Watch Hill Therapy, told Nice News. “If a caregiver is consistently supportive, a child learns that relationships are safe. If a caregiver is inconsistent, distant, or intimidating, a child learns defense mechanisms in order to survive.” These early, deeply ingrained patterns shape how we read people, manage conflict, and regulate emotions, resulting in specific “attachment styles” that we hold onto into adulthood, Rolnick explained. Those of us with a secure attachment style usually find it easier to nurture and sustain close connections, while those with insecure attachment styles (avoidant, anxious, or disorganized) often have trouble in adult relationships. But the good news is that it’s entirely possible to change your patterns. We spoke to Rolnick and three other experts to help us understand the four attachment styles, including how they develop and what you can do to form more secure relationship habits with friends, family, and romantic partners moving forward. Understanding the 4 Attachment Styles Avoidant We might develop an avoidant attachment style if our primary caregiver was emotionally distant or dismissive, per Utah State University . This attachment style can also occur if we were regularly and unreasonably depended on or criticized as a child, Hider Shaaban , a licensed clinical psychologist and founding executive director of Philadelphia Center for Psychotherapy, told Nice News. “So [they] may develop a core belief of ‘If I let people get close to me, they will drain me, judge me, and maybe even hurt me along the way, so it’s safer that I keep my distance.’” Adults with avoidant attachment styles prioritize independence and self-reliance over close connection, added Terri DiMatteo , a licensed professional counselor at Open Door Therapy. “Deep emotional intimacy or vulnerability feels uncomfortable to them,” she said. “When a romantic or non-romantic person gets too close, they are likely to pull away and create distance. Avoidantly attached adults have great difficulty expressing their own emotions, and in the back of their mind is the refrain ‘I don’t need anyone. I am good on my own.’” fizkes—iStock/Getty Images Plus According to the Cleveland Clinic , other potential signs of avoidant attachment include: A strong sense of independence Difficulty trusting people Avoiding physical or emotional intimacy Feeling uncomfortable when people try to get close Being dismissive of others Commitment issues Anxious If you had an inconsistent or emotionally unpredictable caregiver, you might have developed an anxious attachment style, explained Emily Bly , a licensed clinical psychologist and CEO of Psychology Partners Group. When parents “are particularly inconsistent in their emotional responses — vacillating between warm and connected at some moments and cold, nonresponsive, and detached in other moments — [it] can result in the child internalizing a sense that they are ‘not good enough’ or to blame in some way.” Bly added that people with anxious attachment styles tend to fear abandonment and worry that a loved one could withdraw their affection at any time and without warning. They frequently seek reassurance and have trouble believing that people really care for them, and are often on high alert for potential signs of dismissal or rejection. For instance, they might interpret a partner’s subtle shift in tone or a friend’s delayed text response as a signal that something is wrong in the relationship. According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of anxious attachment include: Feeling unworthy of love Difficulty spending time alone High sensitivity to criticism Jealous tendencies Low self-esteem Trouble trusting people Fear of abandonment or rejection Disorganized A disorganized attachment style (also known as fearful avoidant) can occur if a primary caregiver is dangerous or violent. If a parent consistently frightens a child, the child has nowhere to turn in times of distress, Bly explained. As a result, they may develop a “freeze” response to emotional turmoil, feeling that they can’t escape or rely upon their parent. In adulthood, they may shut down and “quasi-dissociate” when stressed, making it difficult for someone else to reach them emotionally, she continued. Relationships can therefore be confusing, as it may feel like the fearful avoidant-attached person has one foot on the gas and another on the brakes. Igor Suka—E+/Getty Images “A person with disorganized attachment craves security and attachment like anyone else, but the fear embedded in this longing will sometimes put the person in a state of ‘system overload,’” Bly said, “where they might be more likely to disappear or ‘ghost’ the attachment figure who tries to get too close to them.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of disorganized attachment include: Difficulty trusting others Trouble with emotional regulation Fear of rejection Confusing, contradictory behaviors Other traits of anxious and avoidant attachments Secure When caregivers provide consistent predictability, abundant love, clear expectations, and straightforward communication, children are often more likely to develop secure attachments. “Basically, they will start to develop the belief system that ‘relationships are generally safe,’ which will help them establish connections with others without the worry of being rejected,” Shaaban said. When they do experience rejection, he added, they’re less likely to take it personally and can bounce back more quickly. People with secure attachment typically view themselves and others positively, communicate honestly and openly, and find it easier to build and maintain lasting, healthy bonds, according to Utah State University. DiMatteo agreed: “Securely attached relationships are safe, relaxed, reliable, and supportive, allowing each person to be their authentic self, knowing they are accepted and valued as they are.” According to the Cleveland Clinic, signs of secure attachment include: Finding it easy to trust others Effective communication Emotional regulation Feeling comfortable spending time alone Finding it easy to connect with others Healthy conflict resolution Being emotionally available to other people How to Become More Secure If you’re prone to forming avoidant, anxious, or disorganized attachments, you can develop an “earned secure” attachment style through healthy adult relationships, positive life experiences, and working with a therapist, per the Cleveland Clinic . Seeing a mental health professional experienced in attachment theory and relationships is especially important if you have a history of trauma, Shaaban noted. You can also try the following to develop healthier, more secure relationship patterns. Understand Your Story: Think about your early childhood and how you developed an insecure attachment style, Bly said. Recognize that your caregiver’s faults, such as inconsistency or emotional distance, reflect their own struggles and have nothing to do with you. With that knowledge, you can begin to rewrite your internal narrative and develop a healthier view of yourself and other people. Seek Out Stable, Secure Relationships: “Be purposeful about seeking out and establishing connections with people who are emotionally mature, consistent, and grounded,” DiMatteo advised. Observing and interacting with securely attached people — including friends, a romantic partner, or a therapist — can help you understand what healthy relationship patterns look like, aiding you in eventually adopting similar behaviors. andreswd—E+/Getty Images Identify Your Triggers: Note the situations that activate your emotional defense mechanisms. “Track your thoughts, bodily sensations, and immediate coping mechanisms when triggered,” Rolnick said. “Writing down your patterns helps you understand yourself rather than running on autopilot.” Practice Honest, Open Communication: Secure attachment involves clear, direct, and authentic interactions with others, and Rolnick suggests working on this by sharing a vulnerable feeling or need with someone you trust once a week. “Vulnerability means something different for every person, and it’s important to gently push your window of tolerance. You might say ‘I felt anxious when I didn’t hear back from you for a few days,’ or ‘I’m having a hard day and feeling anxious — can we talk?’ Each time you face your fear directly, you build your ability to handle similar challenges in the future.” RELATED: Dealing With a Difficult Relationship? Here’s How Psychology Says You Can Shift the Dynamic

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the University of Chicago have identified a mechanism to make immune cells reprogrammed by radiation therapy attack tumors rather than protect them. The study, published in Cancer Cell, shows that radiation activates a protein called TET2 on immune cells in bone marrow, where it removes chemical tags from RNA and locks these cells into an immune-suppressing state.

items.descriptionOriginal: Tin is able to exchange four electrons as it changes between dissolved ions and solid metal, but acidic tin batteries commonly use only a two-electron reaction, leaving half that potential charge out of reach. Now, researchers in China have shown that changing the liquid around the tin could capture that extra capacity.

Καταγόμενος από το χωριό Ράντι, ο Purav άρχισε να δημιουργεί βίντεο με λίγα περισσότερα από το τηλέφωνό του και την ικανότητά του να κάνει τους ανθρώπους να γελούν. items.descriptionOriginal: From a small village in Bihar to screens across India, Purav Jha turned a phone, a passion for acting and a dream into a growing career. Coming from Ranti village, Purav started creating videos with little more than his phone and his ability to make people laugh. But success didn't come overnight. Views were low, recognition was limited, and turning his passion into a career was far from easy. Still, he kept showing up. From playing Poplu to earning recognition as India's “Human AI,” Purav built his identity through performances, comic timing and consistency. Today, his journey from online content creation to acting on OTT platforms reflects years of effort that began far away from the spotlight. His story is a reminder that you don't need an extraordinary beginning to build something meaningful. Sometimes, you just need the courage to keep creating when nobody is watching. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.

items.descriptionOriginal: Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by diabetic retinopathy, a complication of diabetes that affects the eyes. The condition is caused by damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. At first, diabetic retinopathy might not cause any symptoms, or the problems might be mild. However, if the underlying diabetes remains poorly managed, it can lead to blindness.

items.title: Γιατί μια κοινότητα Gond Adivasi θυμάται 2 τίγρεις ως προστάτες του νοικοκυριού

items.description: Για γενιές, μια ιστορία για δύο τίγρεις έχει ταξιδέψει στα νοικοκυριά Gond στο τοπίο Kanha της Madhya Pradesh. Τους έλεγαν Ram και Laxman. Σύμφωνα με την προφορική παράδοση που θυμάται ο Dayal Singh Kusre, ένας Gond Adivasi που εργαζόταν ως μάγειρας σε διάφορα μέρη της Kanha, οι τίγρεις κάποτε μοιράζονταν ένα νοικοκυριό με τους ανθρώπους. Ο κόσμος τα τάισε, κέρασε…
items.descriptionOriginal: For generations, a story about two tigers has travelled through Gond households in Madhya Pradesh's Kanha landscape. They were called Ram and Laxman. According to the oral tradition remembered by Dayal Singh Kusre, a Gond Adivasi who worked as a cook in different parts of Kanha, the tigers once shared a household with people. People fed them, treated them with respect, and regarded them as protectors. The story survives in community memory, along with a practice of making offerings to tigers. It is not a scientific account of tiger behaviour. For Kusre, the story is inseparable from a larger understanding of nature. "Forests and wildlife are not something to be protected from a distance. Both are part of a shared landscape, where people must learn how to live alongside other species", Kusre tells The Better India. But can cultural memory really help people negotiate their place alongside wild animals? When tigers were part of the household Kusre recalls a Gond tribal story in which Ram and Laxman occupied a place within the household's collective memory. According to the Gond folklore, family members were instructed not to encounter the tigers when they first entered the household. A newly married bride, in particular, was told not to open a particular locked room or door. Tigers are elusive, and their presence in a landscape does not necessarily mean that people regularly see them. Photograph: (Videograb-The Corbett Foundation; Dasra India) The restriction was associated with the belief that the tigers would not recognise a new family member, much as traditional households have sometimes maintained rules around interactions between younger women and senior male relatives. In the story, one daughter-in-law eventually opened the door without knowing or following the instructions. She saw the tiger's face, and the animal left the household. Kusre recounts the tiger's message to the family's eldest man: he would now stay in the forest and receive his food there. The room and its closed door represent a boundary that members of the household were expected to respect. The tiger was part of the story, but so was the responsibility of people to recognise that a relationship with wildlife came with limits. The tradition also carries an idea of reciprocity. Kusre says, "The family believed that if people had food, they should ensure that the wildlife around them was fed, too" He also describes a practice of making an offering of a goat or a hen to the tiger in the forest once a year, with the belief that the animal would continue to protect the family. 'Nature is our all' For Kusre, reverence for Ram and Laxman is part of a wider relationship with nature. "For us, nature is our all; we bow at her feet," he says. "If we have to cross 10 km of forests also, then we pray to nature, and the Adivasis feel confident. They trust nature for protection." He also recalls what he describes as older Gond beliefs about encounters with tigers. "Our ancestors used to cross paths with tigers normally, but in reality, tiger spotting is difficult," he says. Tigers are elusive, and their presence in a landscape does not necessarily mean that people regularly see them. These details belong to Kusre's account of Gond oral tradition , but it does not suggest that people should approach, feed, or attempt to house wild tigers today. The meanings communities attach to an animal can also influence whether its continued presence is regarded as valuable. Photograph: (The Corbett Foundation; Dasra India) Its relevance lies in what the narrative reveals about the values through which tribal communities understand the natural world. What communities learn from living alongside wildlife Conservation biologist Shivangi Bendre, whose work focuses primarily on the Central Indian landscape, and mitigating human-wildlife conflict, says it is important to understand the everyday practices through which communities adapt to the presence of wild animals. "I think it is important to look not just at the living practices of communities, but also at their livelihoods and the different, sometimes ingenious, ways they have developed to live alongside wildlife. These practices emerge from generations of experience of sharing landscapes with wild animals," she tells The Better India. Bendre points to communities living alongside sloth bears in Hampi as an example. Drawing insights from Wildlife Conservation Society India's report "A relational perspective of Sloth Bear - Human Relations in Hampi region of Karnataka" by Mohammed Hisham K, she says, 'when sloth bears enter an area, people may light fires, clap or make sounds to alert the animals to their presence." "The idea is to communicate, in a way the animals can recognise, that people are present . Rather than reacting when an encounter happens, community members use these practices to signal their presence and reduce the likelihood of a surprise encounter," she explains. These practices or stories should not automatically be treated as universally effective or safe. Their usefulness depends on the species, local conditions, and the circumstances of an encounter. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Harsha Tej | Lake Conservation, Planting Trees & Farming 🌍 (@muddyfingerss) Still, Bendre says that the knowledge developed by people who live alongside wildlife deserves consideration in conservation planning. Their experiences can help researchers understand how encounters happen, what people fear and which locally developed responses may help reduce risks. When a feared animal becomes part of culture Bendre also points to Pilivesha, a traditional tiger dance practised in Karnataka, as an example of how cultural expression can shape the way people relate to wildlife. In Pilivesha, performers portray tigers through dance and elaborate body painting. The animal becomes part of a public cultural expression, represented through movement, performance and artistic skill. "What is interesting is how such cultural practices can shape the way people relate to an animal that might otherwise evoke fear," Bendre says. In the context she describes, the tradition has helped make the tiger more familiar as a cultural symbol, with some reduction in the fear associated with its presence. Research by Rohan Sharma of WCS India, " Celebrating Nature-Culture Relationships: Documenting Cultures and Traditions of Tiger Folklore in Coastal Karnataka through the Annual Pilivesha Celebrations" , also offers context to this relationship. The research explores how the tradition does not mean that it necessarily reduces conflict with wild tigers, or that cultural familiarity can substitute for practical safety measures. It shows how an animal's place in community life can extend beyond the risks associated with encounters. Dikesh Chaudhary, project officer at The Corbett Foundation, stresses the importance of preserving such traditions as part of community history. "The idea is to save the tradition. It is a challenge, the cultural part. It is part of the history of the Gond and Baiga communities, and it is thus important," he says. For Chaudhary, these traditions also offer a response to a question that can arise in conservation discussions: why should tigers be protected? "There are people who still may have questions: 'Baagh kyun bachana hai?' (Why should we save the tiger? This is the answer to that question. We should know why we need to save the tiger." Communities need reliable information about animal behaviour, practical guidance on reducing encounters and access to appropriate support when incidents occur. Photograph: (Apoorva Jadon) Cultural traditions cannot, on their own, explain every ecological reason for conserving a species. Tigers play a role in forest ecosystems, and their protection is connected to the wider conservation of habitats and biodiversity. But the meanings communities attach to an animal can also influence whether its continued presence is regarded as valuable. Are all traditional beliefs good for conservation? Respecting cultural memory does not mean accepting every traditional belief without question. Some beliefs may discourage the killing of animals or encourage people to regard wildlife as worthy of protection. Others may have little direct bearing on conservation. And some can create risks for people, particularly when a belief influences decisions during a medical emergency. Where wildlife-related risks affect livelihoods or safety, conservation efforts must also take those everyday realities seriously. Photograph: (Sangeetha Balaji) Bendre talks about this distinction through an example she encountered in studies in Kanha, where a belief about snakebite can influence how people respond after being bitten. "The belief is that there's this one particular jari-booti(medicinal herb) that, when the person who's been bitten consumes it, the snake, wherever it is, will die and split into two halves," she says. According to Bendre, people who believe in this remedy may turn to traditional healers rather than take the person who has been bitten to a hospital. The problem, she explains, is not that the belief exists. It is that following it may delay treatment and put the person's life at risk. "They're not really directly attacking the snake, but at the same time, that superstition may cause the person's life to be in danger," she says. A belief that does not directly encourage people to kill a snake may have a different conservation implication from one that delays potentially life-saving medical care. The question, therefore, is not whether traditional beliefs should be accepted or rejected wholesale. It is how to recognise their significance while addressing practices that create risks. Awareness is only part of the answer "Education and awareness and primary healthcare is also something that needs to be addressed in parallel with whatever awareness that we do on the conservation front," Bendre says. Communities need reliable information about animal behaviour, practical guidance on reducing encounters and access to appropriate support when incidents occur. Where wildlife-related risks affect livelihoods or safety, conservation efforts must also take those everyday realities seriously. The story of Ram and Laxman cannot tell us how tigers behave, whether they recognise people as family or whether feeding an animal will make it a protector. Those questions require evidence, and the story should not be treated as a guide to interacting with wild tigers. In Kusre's telling, the tigers' departure from the household does not end the relationship. The story continues through remembrance, reverence, and the belief that the forest remains their place. Its central idea is not that wild animals should live with people, but that people must recognise their place in a landscape they share with other species. Coexistence does not mean eliminating every boundary between humans and wildlife. It means finding ways to live alongside animals while respecting their ecological needs and protecting human lives.

items.descriptionOriginal: A garden in the middle of a city can be more than a patch of green. Look closely, and you might spot a butterfly moving between flowers, bees hovering over native plants, and children exploring the outdoors at their own pace. These small encounters are part of a much bigger story about biodiversity, belonging and the spaces we make for nature. In Ludhiana, Punjab, 16-year-old Gunisha Kaur is helping bring this vision to life. Through her initiative, Buzzing Blooms, she has established more than 20 pollinator gardens and ecological restoration projects across Ludhiana, Meerut, Mumbai and partner communities. Through Buzzing Blooms, Gunisha is transforming underused urban spaces into chemical-free habitats for bees, butterflies and other pollinators. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) Her work has now earned her third place at the 2026 International Young Eco-Hero Awards , presented by environmental organisation Action For Nature. Over 24 months of monitoring, the gardens recorded a 155% increase in pollinator species richness, from 18 species to 46. Bee visits also increased by nearly 200%, according to the organisation. But for Gunisha, the idea was never just about planting more flowers. It was also about creating outdoor spaces where people with different needs could feel comfortable and connected to nature. How a personal experience inspired Buzzing Blooms Growing up in Ludhiana, an industrialised city, Gunisha became concerned about the declining pollinator populations she observed around her. At the same time, her experiences at home were shaping how she understood the relationship between people and the natural world. Watching her younger autistic brother helped her recognise how calming natural surroundings could be. It also made her aware of how few outdoor spaces were designed to accommodate neurodivergent children and their sensory needs. The gardens feature native plants, structured pathways and touch-safe greenery to make nature more accessible to children with different sensory needs. Photograph: (Instagram/ @ gunisha_eco ) These observations led her to launch Buzzing Blooms on 5 March 2023, with a vision to transform underused urban spaces into chemical-free habitats that support both biodiversity and inclusion. Her Sikh heritage, which emphasises respect for nature, also informs her approach. "Rooted in my culture, which teaches respect for nature, I was inspired to create spaces that nurture both biodiversity and belonging," she adds. Gardens designed for bees, butterflies and children At Buzzing Blooms, the idea of a successful garden extends beyond how it looks. The spaces use layers of native plants and chemical-free cultivation methods to create habitats for pollinators, including bees and butterflies. The design also considers the people who visit. Structured pathways make the gardens easier to navigate, while non-thorny, touch-safe plants and designated bee- and butterfly-watching zones allow children to explore nature in ways that suit their sensory needs. The result is an approach that brings ecological restoration and accessibility together, rather than treating them as separate goals. Over 24 months of monitoring, Buzzing Blooms recorded a 155% increase in pollinator species richness, from 18 to 46 species. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) And the impact goes beyond the gardens themselves. Buzzing Blooms has engaged more than 4,000 students, including over 250 neurodivergent and vulnerable individuals. Through workshops, restoration drives and inclusive learning programmes, the initiative has reached more than 8,000 people. Gunisha has also established the Buzzing Blooms Peer Advocacy Network, training more than 500 young ambassadors in environmental communication, public speaking and leadership. To help fund the work, she conducts art classes on weekends and reinvests her earnings, alongside money from plant sales and scholarships, into maintaining the gardens. From local gardens to international recognition Gunisha's interest in finding solutions to environmental challenges also extends to technology. She developed AeroBloom, an artificial-intelligence-guided aerial pollination system designed to support agriculture during extreme heat, when natural pollinators may temporarily leave an area. The innovation earned her a bronze medal at the Indian Science and Engineering Fair. Gunisha Kaur wins third place at the 2026 International Young Eco-Hero Awards for her work with Buzzing Blooms. Photograph: ( Buzzing Blooms ) Her latest recognition at the International Young Eco-Hero Awards puts a spotlight on what a young changemaker can achieve by addressing environmental problems within her own community. From creating habitats for pollinators to making green spaces more welcoming for children, Gunisha's work offers a practical lesson in how cities can become more inclusive while supporting biodiversity. Sources: 'Meet Gunisha Kaur, the 16-year-old from Ludhiana who won third place at the 2026 Internation Young Eco Awards' by The Times Of India, Published ob 16 October 2026. 'Gunisha Kaur' Action For Nature. 'Meet Gunisha Kaur, the 16-year-old eco-hero creating inclusive gardens for pollinators and children across Indian cities' by Trisha Bhattacharya for Live Mint, Published on 17 October 2026.

Η θεματοφύλακας που κουβαλούσε ιδιωτικά την αίσθηση της αποτυχίας ήταν, για όλους γύρω της, η ζωντανή καρδιά του Aubrey Indepe…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton swept floors, bought supplies for children who couldn't afford them, and turned smiles "up instead of down" -- work she once measured against a college degree she never earned and found herself wanting. The custodian who privately carried a sense of failure was, to everyone around her, the living heart of Aubrey Independent School District in Texas. When the superintendent called her to the podium under the pretense of a routine meeting, Hampton unrolled a small red carpet and found her own name printed on it: Marilyn Hampton Elementary School. The next day, she was still crying. "Whoever thought a janitor would have a school named after them," she said, and in that sentence lives the quiet revelation the story holds: that a life spent in faithful, unglamorous service to others can quietly become the most significant thing in a room, in a district, in a community's memory -- long before anyone thinks to say so out loud.

Η αυξημένη κινητικότητα των τελευταίων ημερών συνδέεται, σύμφωνα με τους φαρμακοποιούς, με την πτώση της θερμοκρασίας, ενώ η επάρκεια των εμβολίων στα φαρμακεία παραμένει εξασφαλισμένη. Όπως ανέφερε στο ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ ο γενικός γραμματέας του Πανελλήνιου Φαρμακευτικού Συλλόγου (ΠΦΣ), Μανόλης Κατσαράκης, περισσότερες από εννέα στις δέκα δόσεις χορηγούνται μέσω των φαρμακείων. Για τη φετινή περίοδο έχουν εισαχθεί συνολικά 3,64 εκατομμύρια δόσεις, το μεγαλύτερο μέρος των οποίων έχει ήδη διοχετευθεί στα φαρμακεία. Η διαδικασία εξαρτάται από τον τύπο του εμβολίου. Το συμβατικό αντιγριπικό εμβόλιο διατίθεται στα φαρμακεία με τη χρήση του ΑΜΚΑ, χωρίς να χρειάζεται προηγουμένως συνταγή γιατρού. Η δυνατότητα αυτή ισχύει τόσο για ασφαλισμένους όσο και για ανασφάλιστους. Διαφορετική είναι η διαδικασία για το ενισχυμένο εμβόλιο, το οποίο προορίζεται για συγκεκριμένες κατηγορίες ατόμων άνω των 65 ετών και απαιτεί ιατρική συνταγογράφηση. Πότε […]

items.descriptionOriginal: Ο Γιάννης Στάνκογλου και ο Κρατερός Κατσούλης πρωταγωνιστούν σε ένα από τα πιο αγαπημένα και πολυβραβευμένα κωμικά μιούζικαλ του παγκόσμιου θεάτρου, (ανάμεσά τους έξι βραβεία Tony), το θρυλικό «Κλουβί με τις Τρελές» (La Cage aux Folles), που έχει κατακτήσει τις μεγαλύτερες θεατρικές σκηνές του κόσμου, το οποίο ανεβαίνει στη σκηνή του ιστορικού Θεάτρου Βέμπο. Χρησιμοποιώντας μικροσκοπικούς ανθρώπινους αμφιβληστροειδή που αναπτύχθηκαν στο εργαστήριο, οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν ότι ένα παράγωγο της βιταμίνης Α και οι ορμόνες του θυρεοειδούς συνεργάζονται για να διαμορφώσουν το foveola, το ti…
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.

items.titleOriginal: ‘India Felt Like One Giant, Compassionate Family’: A Couple's 80-Day Motorcycle Journey Around the Country
