Αλλά ξέραμε ότι αν συνεχίζαμε να περιμένουμε την κατάλληλη στιγμή, μπορεί να μην πάμε ποτέ." Για τον Samrat Ulhas Dambe (30) και τη σύζυγό του Varshali Samrat Dambe (35) η απώλεια της δουλειάς τους το 2024 έφερε στο επίκεντρο ένα αβέβαιο μέλλον. Είχαν δουλέψει και οι δύο…
items.descriptionOriginal: "We didn't know if we had enough money to complete the journey. We did not even know what we would do when we came back. But we knew that if we kept waiting for the right time, we might never go." For Samrat Ulhas Dambe (30) and his wife Varshali Samrat Dambe (35) losing their jobs in 2024 brought an uncertain future into focus. Both had worked in the corporate world, building careers and following familiar routines . Then, around June that year, they were laid off. With a few months ahead of them and no solid idea of what came next, they began thinking about a dream they had carried for years. Could they ride along India's borders on their motorcycle? The idea had been with Samrat since he was 12, when he would draw the outline of India and imagine tracing its borders on a bike. Over the years, it became a dream the couple shared. They had been riding together since 2018 and bought a Benelli TRK in 2022, hoping to take on longer adventures. Now, with time on their hands but limited savings, they decided to attempt the journey, which they called the 'Art India Ride'. On 19 September 2024, they left their home in Mhapral, a village in Maharashtra's Ratnagiri district, about 150 kilometres from Mumbai. They would spend the next 80 days travelling 16,428 km, covering 22 states and four Union Territories, through deserts, mountain passes, remote border settlements, and unfamiliar roads. They returned home on 8 December 2024, having completed a journey they had once thought they might only manage halfway. In January 2025, their achievement was recognised by the India Book of Records as IBR Achiever 2025. But the record was only one part of the story. Along the way, the couple faced freezing temperatures, tight budgets, and moments when they wondered whether they should turn back. They also found strangers who welcomed them into their homes, fed them, and treated them like family. When the time finally felt right Before the journey, Samrat worked as a digital marketing expert at a multinational company, while Varshali was a digital marketing manager at a digital agency. Their lives revolved around work and the usual plans people make for the future. They had been riding together since 2018 and bought a Benelli TRK in 2022, hoping to take on longer adventures. The layoffs in June 2024 left them with uncertainty, but also something they rarely had before. Time. "We suddenly had three to four months available, and we didn't know exactly what we were going to do next," the husband tells The Better India . "It was an uncertain phase, but we began to see it as an opportunity to do something we had always wanted to do." Samrat's dream of riding around India's borders had never really gone away. The couple had already spent years riding together, and the idea of taking on the country's outer reaches felt like a natural next step. By August, they had decided to go ahead. They did not have enough savings to be certain they could complete the whole route. At first, they thought they might travel through only half of India. Still, they did not want to keep postponing the dream until their finances were more comfortable. "If we waited for the perfect financial moment, we knew life would get in the way, and the dream might fade. We decided to start and see how far our resources would take us," Varshali adds. There was one last change before departure. They had initially planned to travel south first, but heavy rainfall across South India prompted them to rethink the route. With just eight days to go, they decided to begin in Gujarat and travel clockwise around the country instead. On 19 September, they set off from Mhapral, carrying excitement, nervousness, and no guarantee of how far they would get. Five bags and a budget to stretch The couple knew that completing the journey would require careful spending. Their Benelli TRK averaged around 20 km per litre, so fuel was a major expense. They set a daily limit of Rs 3,500 for fuel, food and accommodation, and generally looked for rooms costing no more than Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,500 a night. They ate at small local eateries and kept their stays simple. The couple had no elaborate itinerary mapping out every day. Instead, they usually decided their next halt and route only a day or two in advance. "We wanted to remain flexible. Weather, road conditions and accommodation could change our plans at any time," she explains. That flexibility had already proved useful when they changed their route before setting off. It also gave them the freedom to travel places they had not known much about before reaching them. Packing was another exercise in deciding what they could do without. For 80 days, their belongings fitted into five bags. Each had a saddlebag for clothes and personal items. A top box carried their laptop, cameras, electronic equipment, and a basic toolkit. Their tank bag held phones, documents and essentials, while an additional bag carried winter layers and raincoats. They travelled with just three T-shirts, two pairs of jeans and their riding gear, along with the equipment they needed for the road. "Travelling with so little taught us that we didn't need as many things as we thought we did," Samrat says. Their money was always part of the calculation. Fuel, food, accommodation, and motorcycle maintenance all had to fit within their means. They had also agreed that if their savings fell to Rs 40,000, they would return home and look for jobs. That possibility meant every stretch of road carried a question . Could they afford to keep going? Would the weather cooperate? Where would they sleep that night? Now, with time on their hands but limited savings, they decided to attempt the journey, which they called the 'Art India Ride'. They decided to continue riding, figuring out the road ahead as they went. The road tested them before it rewarded them Their route took them from Maharashtra through Gujarat and Rajasthan, then Haryana and Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. They continued through Chandigarh, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, before reaching West Bengal and Sikkim. From there, they rode through Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Meghalaya, then followed the eastern coast through Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. After reaching Kanyakumari, they turned back north through Kerala, Karnataka and Goa, completing their journey in Maharashtra. The first few days were harder than they had imagined. Near Santalpur, around the Gujarat-Rajasthan border, they crossed a long, isolated stretch without seeing another person. A storm rolled in, the power went out, and the area began to feel unfamiliar. The only hotel they could find was surrounded by parked trucks, with only truck drivers stopping there for the night. Samrat grew anxious and began wondering whether they should turn back. Varshali encouraged him to continue. It was a difficult moment, not because the couple had suddenly stopped believing in their dream, but because they were realising what it meant to pursue it without knowing what lay ahead. Ladakh brought another set of challenges. They reached the high-altitude region in October, when the tourist season was winding down, and many hotels had closed. Around Pangong Lake, temperatures dropped to minus 12 degrees Celsius. They had not ridden in Ladakh before and had not fully anticipated how harsh the conditions could be. Poor network connectivity, difficult roads and the remoteness of some stretches added to their worries. They were also concerned about getting a puncture on their motorcycle's tube tyres in places where help could be difficult to find. At Upshi, the cold became particularly difficult for Varshali, who was shivering. They eventually found a local Maharashtrian who helped them arrange a room with a heater. The experience taught them to adjust quickly, look out for each other and accept help when they needed it. There were no guarantees that the next day would be easier, but they learnt to deal with one challenge at a time. The strangers who made them feel at home For the couple, the most memorable parts of the journey were the people they met rather than the places they saw. In Punjab, a family welcomed them into their home and insisted they stay as guests. In Tawang, Arunachal Pradesh, a woman from Maharashtra who lived there offered them prayers and blessings for the road ahead, greeting them with a traditional Tibetan white shawl. In Bhalukpong, they met an elderly couple who ran a cafe. The two travellers formed a warm connection with the uncle, who treated Samrat with the affection he might show his own son. When the couple returned to see him on their way back, he became emotional as they prepared to leave. Thousands of kilometres from home, they found people willing to make space for them, share what they had and offer encouragement without expecting anything in return. Their journey also gave them a closer view of life in remote border regions and the work of the Indian Army and the Border Security Force. They came away with a stronger appreciation of the people who live in difficult conditions and those who serve in them. "Before the journey, India was a map of different states, languages, food, and cultures," the husband explains. "After travelling 16,428 kilometres, it felt like one giant, compassionate family. The warmth we received from people remained largely similar, wherever we went." One encounter in North Bengal brought home just how far a journey can reach beyond the people making it. Travelling from Sikkim towards Jaigaon in West Bengal, the couple stopped at a small stall for breakfast. A group of people arrived by car and noticed the Maharashtra registration on their motorcycle. Curious about how far they had travelled, they invited the couple to sit with them and talk. The conversation lasted nearly two hours. One of the men, Arun Sircar, a corporate professional from Kolkata, explained why he had been asking so many questions. "Once upon a time, this was my dream too. I moved to the USA, worked hard, and bought a luxury BMW because I wanted to travel. My wife and I wanted to live life on the road, just like you. But somehow, life caught up with us, and we got stuck," he says. He had driven across the United States but had never experienced his own country in the way the couple was doing. "You are living my dream, bro. Through your journey, I feel like I am travelling too," he told them. The couple knew that completing the journey would require careful spending. The words moved Samrat and Varshali. Their ride had begun as a personal ambition , but here was someone who felt connected to it because it represented a life he had once imagined for himself. Sircar and his wife invited the couple to their home. She prepared a vegetarian feast despite not having cooked vegetarian food before, and they invited friends over to hear about the journey. The couple were also given a room for the night. For the travelling duo, the connection became a reminder that a journey could mean something to people who had never taken the same road themselves. What the road taught them Kaushal Sethia, a 26-year-old software engineer from Surat, had met the couple in Naggar, Himachal Pradesh, where they were neighbours at a homestay. They spent almost a month together and became close friends. When the duo began their border expedition, Sethia and his family followed their progress and regularly asked for updates. What stayed with him was not just the distance they covered. "The way they support each other is what makes the journey special. It tests you physically, mentally, and emotionally. The most difficult part of a journey is starting, and they didn't just start it. They completed it against all the problems," he says. The 80 days had tested the couple's relationship, too. Sharing a motorcycle, limited belongings and constant uncertainty meant making decisions together, managing tiredness and adapting to changing conditions. They learnt to recognise when one of them needed encouragement, rest or a little space. For Samrat, riding also became a way of silencing the noise in his head. "When you are on a motorcycle for days at a time, the beat of the engine and the focus the road demands bring you into the present moment," he says. "For me, it feels like meditation." The couple returned to Mhapral on 8 December 2024, after spending 80 days on the road. Their total expenditure came to around Rs 3.75 lakh, covering fuel, food, accommodation, repairs, and maintenance. They had completed the journey without knowing at the outset whether their savings would last. They had also returned with memories of people who had made the road feel less lonely. They were not thinking about a record while travelling. After reaching Goa, a friend suggested that they apply to the India Book of Records. They submitted photographs, fuel receipts, and other documents for verification, and in January 2025, they were recognised as IBR Achiever 2025. The recognition was welcome, but the couple say the people they met and what they learnt mattered more than the certificate. Their route took them from Maharashtra through Gujarat and Rajasthan, then Haryana and Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. Carrying the journey forward On 6 April 2025, Samrat and Varshali started 'Souls of Motorcycle', a riding community inspired by what the Art India Ride had taught them. They wanted to create a space for motorcycle enthusiasts to learn, travel responsibly and experience the road as more than a test of speed, distance or engine capacity. The community has grown to more than 700 members, with over 8,000 Instagram followers. The couple organise rides to destinations such as Ladakh and Sikkim and are working to expand into cities including Surat, Chandigarh, Kolkata, and Bengaluru. Their aim is to help more people become confident riders, discover places they might not otherwise visit and find some mental space away from their everyday routines. For the couple, riding is not only about reaching a destination. It is also about being present, meeting people and returning with a different perspective on life. The Art India Ride gave them a way to experience that for themselves, and Souls of Motorcycle is how they now hope to share it with others. Their journey began at a moment when the future felt uncertain. They had lost their jobs, their savings were limited and they could not be sure they would complete the route. But rather than waiting for life to become predictable, they chose to begin. They rode through freezing nights and lonely stretches, accepted help from strangers and experienced how much could happen when two people kept moving towards the same goal. The record gave their journey a number. The people they met gave it meaning. And the dream that began with a boy drawing the outline of India became 16,428 kilometres of road, shared courage, and a reminder that sometimes the right time is the time you decide to start. All pictures courtesy Varshali Dambe.

items.title: Τι κάνει τη Scary Music Scary; Ο συνθέτης "Obsession" για τη δημιουργία μιας ταινίας τρόμου δολοφονίας
items.titleOriginal: What Makes Scary Music Scary? The “Obsession” Composer on Crafting a Killer Horror Movie Score
items.description: Στο δεύτερο μισό της ταινίας The Shining του Stanley Kubrick, υπάρχει μια εμβληματική σεκάνς που είναι αναμφισβήτητα τόσο τρομακτική όσο η έξαψη με τσεκούρι του Jack Nicholson. Ξεκινά ήσυχα, η κάμερα ακολουθεί τη Shelley Duvall καθώς περπατά προς ένα σκιερό δωμάτιο. Τα βήματά της αντηχούν στη σιωπή προτού εισέλθει ένας δυσοίωνος ήχος, σχεδόν σαν παραμορφωμένος λευκός θόρυβος. Ο…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the second half of Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining , there’s an iconic sequence that’s arguably as terrifying as Jack Nicholson’s ax-wielding rampage. It begins quietly, the camera following Shelley Duvall as she walks toward a shadowy room. Her footsteps echo in the silence before an ominous sound creeps in, almost like distorted white noise. The music builds, getting louder and more complex as warped high notes slowly penetrate the din. It’s chaotic, dissonant, deafening, mirroring the emotions on Duvall’s face, until finally, finally — well, we won’t give you any spoilers . “If you watched it on mute, I don’t know if it would feel nearly as scary,” Rock Burwell told Nice News of the classic flick. Burwell composed the score for this year’s breakout indie horror film, Obsession , which raked in $500 million-plus off a $750,000 budget, making it the highest-grossing movie ever produced for under $1 million. The Los Angeles-based composer recognizes how essential music is to evoking emotion in filmgoers, and his eerie orchestration played an outsize role in Obsession’s success. “What just generally has always drawn me to music in the first place is its ability to influence how we feel,” he said. But what exactly makes scary music scary? We may all have some general idea of the characteristics of creepy music — the crescendo of staccato strings in Psycho ’s shower scene comes to mind — but the way in which a score achieves its effect varies greatly. There are certain common elements, however, that lend themselves to disconcerting an audience. Subverting Expectations For Obsession , Burwell — after discussions with writer-director Curry Barker — chose a nontraditional approach, opting to subtly discomfit viewers through dreamy, nostalgic melodies, slightly pitch-bending his notes and drenching everything in reverb. “It was fun to explore not coming in with these really harsh, interval, screechy-sounding kind of things that you hear in a lot of horror movies,” he explained, “but actually coming from something that feels a bit more warm and almost comforting. But the way it moves and is undulating underneath is very — it kind of gets under your skin a little bit more.” Composer Katy Jarzebowski , who recently scored the award-winning documentary Gaslit featuring Jane Fonda, has been working in the industry for over 20 years. She noted that today’s savvy audiences are well-versed in the language of film. The key to unsettling them, then, is to present a musical choice they don’t necessarily understand or expect. “If you give them something that they know and love, then it kind of takes that feeling of discomfort away,” she explained, adding: “[When filmmakers] don’t give them something that they expect, it becomes uncomfortable.” Tension Tension is the heart of any horror film, and a good one typically leaves viewers on tenterhooks throughout. To that end, Burwell noted that the descending melodies and drawn-out cues he used can cause audiences to feel as though they’re suspended, waiting for a resolution that never comes. “Everything is very, like, ambient and long, and it’s slow moving,” he said. “I think that the pace of it really allows those feelings to sit in a bit longer.” He added that he’s heard from fans that the sweet-yet-tainted score had them feeling “very comforted, but at the same time, feeling kind of bad or that there’s something missing or that there’s yearning.” Jarzebowski agreed with the idea of holding out on viewers. “It’s a lot about where you choose to come in or where you choose to hold back,” she said. “You know, a lot of times [it’s] not giving that kind of pillow for the audience to land on to remind them that they’re in a movie in the first place.” In the Studio Pete Horner is an Emmy-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer at Skywalker Sound (who also happens to be married to Jarzebowski). He pointed out that the terror conveyed through a horror movie’s sound isn’t merely from the music itself. Foley is the art of creating sound effects in a studio — things like footsteps or a door creaking — and Horner said it can be used to great effect for inducing fear in quiet scenes. “By accentuating those things, it kind of draws you closer to the action, and it makes you feel uncomfortable because you shouldn’t be able to hear that,” he explained, adding: “It mimics what happens when you are scared, which is that you become hyperaware of your surroundings. And when you’re not scared, you probably don’t hear the footsteps at all, even though they are happening in the space you’re in. But if you are scared, every little tiny sound has huge meaning.” Additionally, gradually removing the ambient background noise (called “room tone”) from a scene can be extremely disconcerting. “It’s something you want to use sparingly in a movie, but if you pull out of all of the ambiences, the effect that it has is the audience will hold their breath,” Horner said. “Because they’re listening, they’re trying to hear into the sound, and there’s nothing there. And it’s a very scary feeling.” Working With the Cinematography It’s typical for musicians to score to picture, meaning they create the music as they watch the film. But sometimes, the two arts inform each other more equally. In Obsession , Burwell sent early cues to Barker while he and director of photography Taylor Clemons were coming up with the shot list. Barker later told Burwell that playing the music on set really helped establish the mood they were going for. Likewise, watching Clemons’ claustrophobic cinematography influenced Burwell’s choices for the score. “We kind of leaned on the darkness, like, there’s not much high frequency information in the music, and there’s not a whole lot of light in a lot of these scenes, too,” Burwell said. “I’ve kind of referred to it as a lot of the score feeling like a lead blanket or something like that. Like, it’s just really heavy. And I think the cinematography really informed that for me.” Experimentation Starting with what’s considered the first-ever horror flick (a three-minute silent French film from 1896 titled The Haunted Castle ) to the dozens coming out in 2027 , the genre is a confirmed favorite of moviegoers. Call it sublimation or call it masochism, but people like to be scared. And that means composers have ample opportunity — and one could say the imperative — to get creative. “Horror is a great place for composers, especially to experiment with different things because a lot of times, you’re trying to create a fear that someone doesn’t know yet,” Jarzebowski said, adding: “We already have Psycho , we have Stranger Things , we have [horror filmmaker and composer John] Carpenter — all this horror language that we’ve created. So you already know what to be scared of. So there’s always room for, like, ‘OK, what else can we do to make it even scarier? What haven’t they heard yet?’”

items.title: Αυτά είναι μερικά από τα πράγματα που είναι πιο πιθανό να κάνουν τους ανθρώπους να ουρλιάζουν
items.titleOriginal: These Are Some of the Things Most Likely to Make People Scream
items.description: Τι σε τρομάζει; Ένας μυστηριώδης γδούπος κάτω στη μέση της νύχτας, να εντοπίσεις μια αράχνη στο μαξιλάρι σου και να νιώθεις κάτι να πιέζει το πόδι σου στη θάλασσα είναι μεταξύ των 10 κορυφαίων πραγμάτων που κάνουν τους Βρετανούς να ουρλιάζουν, σύμφωνα με μια πρόσφατη έρευνα 2.000 ενηλίκων στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο.…
items.descriptionOriginal: What spooks you? A mysterious thud downstairs in the middle of the night, spotting a spider on your pillow, and feeling something brush against your leg in the sea are among the top 10 things that make Brits scream, according to a recent survey of 2,000 adults in the U.K. Yet despite being quick to shriek, the nation appears to embrace the fun side of fear, with 84% of respondents saying scary experiences are more likely to end in laughter than panic when shared with others. More than half also confirmed enjoying spooky thrills in a group setting tends to leave them laughing, particularly when watching horror films, riding roller coasters, or braving a haunted attraction. SWNS According to psychologist Kimberley Wilson, there’s a scientific reason these scary experiences can feel surprisingly enjoyable, something she’s dubbed the “Shared Shriek Effect.” “When we watch something scary, our bodies respond as if we’re facing a threat. Our heart rate increases, adrenaline rises, and our attention sharpens,” she told SWNS. “The difference is that our brains know we’re actually safe, which allows us to experience that physical rush as excitement rather than fear.” Wilson added: “When we share that experience with other people, whether we’re jumping, screaming, or laughing together, it can create a genuine sense of connection. The scream itself also helps release the tension that’s been building up, which is why laughter so often follows.” There are benefits beyond the thrill, too, with a quarter saying that being scared offers an escape from everyday life, while 24% see it as a healthy emotional release. Nearly 1 in 5 of those polled also believe it acts as an instant stress reliever. The research was done via OnePoll and commissioned by M&M’s to mark the launch of the candy brand’s new “ Screaming Service ,” encouraging people to swap streaming for screaming this Halloween. “We think Halloween isn’t really about being scared, it’s about screaming together,” said Georgia Woodward, a senior brand manager at M&M’s. “Our ‘Screaming Service’ celebrates those moments across the month of Halloween when everyone jumps at the same scenes, hides behind a cushion, and ends up laughing together about it afterwards.” Top 10 Things That Make Brits Shriek SWNS 1. Someone unexpectedly jumping out at you as a prank 2. Hearing a knock at the window when it’s dark 3. Hearing a mysterious thud downstairs in the night 4. Missing a step at the bottom of the stairs 5. Spotting a spider on your pillow 6. Feeling something brush against your leg in the sea 7. Seeing a mouse dart across a room 8. Being caught off guard by a spooky film twist 9. Someone unexpectedly shouting “boo!” 10. Walking face-first into a cobweb This article was originally written by Zara Zubeidi for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.title: Πώς ο εγκέφαλός σας σώζει τη νοσταλγία από τα σκάνδαλα
items.titleOriginal: How Your Brain Saves Nostalgia From Scandals
items.description: Μπορείτε να διαχωρίσετε την τέχνη από τον καλλιτέχνη; Μια νέα μελέτη δείχνει ότι ο εγκέφαλός μας το κάνει αυτόματα: όταν ένας αγαπημένος δημιουργός πέφτει από τη χάρη, η μνήμη εκτελεί «ηθική επέμβαση», υποβαθμίζοντας το άτομο ενώ προστατεύει τις νοσταλγικές αναμνήσεις της τέχνης του.
items.descriptionOriginal: Can you separate the art from the artist? A new study shows our brains do it automatically: when a beloved creator falls from grace, memory performs "moral surgery," downgrading the person while protecting nostalgic memories of their art.

items.title: Διατροφική λεκιθίνη που συνδέεται με χαμηλότερη γνωστική εξασθένηση
items.titleOriginal: Dietary Lecithin Linked to Lower Cognitive Impairment
items.description: Μπορεί η καθημερινή διατροφική λεκιθίνη να υπερασπιστεί την απώλεια μνήμης; Μια μελέτη 1.917 ηλικιωμένων ενηλίκων που συνδυάζει αξιολογήσεις MoCA με στοχευμένα λιπιδομικά αποκαλύπτει ότι η λεκιθίνη και η πολυακόρεστη φωσφατιδυλοχολίνη συνδέονται με χαμηλότερα ποσοστά ήπιας γνωστικής εξασθένησης, ιδιαίτερα σε ενήλικες με χαμηλότερη εκπαίδευση.
items.descriptionOriginal: Can everyday dietary lecithin defend against memory loss? A study of 1,917 older adults combining MoCA assessments with targeted lipidomics reveals that lecithin and polyunsaturated phosphatidylcholine are linked to lower rates of mild cognitive impairment, particularly in adults with lower education.

items.titleOriginal: Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug?
items.description: Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν ότι ο εμβολιασμός μητέρων ποντικών μεταφέρει αντισώματα που προστατεύουν τα ευάλωτα νεογνά έναντι της Klebsiella pneumoniae. Η Klebsiella pneumoniae είναι ένα επικίνδυνο βακτήριο που σκοτώνει χιλιάδες βρέφη σε χώρες χαμηλού και μεσαίου εισοδήματος κάθε χρόνο και είναι ο μεγαλύτερος δολοφόνος παιδιών παγκοσμίως. Τέτοιες λοιμώξεις μπορεί να είναι δύσκολες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered that vaccinating mouse mothers transfers antibodies that defend vulnerable newborns against Klebsiella pneumoniae . Klebsiella pneumoniae is a dangerous bacterium that kills thousands of infants in low- and middle-income countries each year and is the leading killer of children globally. Such infections can be difficult to treat due to the bacterium’s growing resistance to antibiotics and there is currently no vaccine available to prevent infection. The study in Science Advances points to a promising new strategy for protecting vulnerable infants from the drug-resistant superbug by harnessing maternal immunity. “ Klebsiella pneumoniae is a serious threat to newborns who have not yet developed their own immune defenses,” says the study’s senior author, David A. Rosen, an associate professor of pediatrics and of molecular microbiology at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. “Our study shows that maternal immunization can effectively bridge that critical window of vulnerability, giving newborns the protection they need right from birth.” K. pneumoniae is a big problem around the world, especially in the hospital where it can cause pneumonia and other infections among adults and children. In low- and middle-income countries, where children often get exposed to the bacterium in their environment, it drives severe bacterial blood infections, known as sepsis. Because K. pneumoniae is increasingly resistant to standard antibiotics, doctors are often left without effective medicines to treat such infections. The Rosen team collaborated with the lab of Drew Schwartz, an assistant professor of pediatrics, to model K. pneumoniae sepsis in newborn mice that mimics the infection seen in children and asked if vaccinating a pregnant mouse would prevent infection in pups. Female mice were immunized at the time of mating and then again once or twice during pregnancy. The vaccine targets two of the most dangerous types of K. pneumoniae —known as K1 and K2—and was developed by Omniose, a St. Louis-based startup. Rosen had previously published findings that show the vaccine is effective in preventing K. pneumoniae infection in adult mice that can progress to life-threatening liver, respiratory tract, bloodstream, and other infections. Two weeks after birth, the young mice were exposed to lethal doses of the bacteria, either the K1 or K2 type. Of the two-week-old mouse pups from unvaccinated mothers, 0% infected with the K1 type and less than 35% with the K2 type survived. In contrast, of the young mice from vaccinated mothers, more than 80% infected with either type survived. Whether the mother received two or three doses of the vaccine did not impact survival. The researchers drew blood weekly from the young mice starting on their day of birth and continuing up to six weeks of life. They also collected breast milk from lactating mice. They found high concentrations of vaccine-specific antibodies in both the milk of vaccinated mothers and their newborn mice over the course of the study. “Mice that were never immunized themselves are highly protected from a lethal infection just from the durable antibodies transferred to them from their mother,” explains first author Paeton Wantuch, a staff scientist in the Rosen lab. The researchers are now testing updated vaccines designed to shield against multiple strains of the superbug found across the globe. “This study presents the first evidence that giving moms a vaccine could be an effective strategy for protecting their babies against these severe infections,” says Rosen. “And it also has established a practical model that we can now use to test therapies and vaccines that will bring us one step closer to human clinical trials with the ultimate goal of impacting global health.” This work was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Gates Foundation, and the Washington University Department of Pediatrics. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official view of the NIH, the Gates Foundation or other funders. Competing Interest Statement: Robinson LS, Darwech I, Knoot CJ, and Harding CM have a financial stake in Omniose, a for-profit entity developing bioconjugate vaccines using patented technology reflected in the data presented in this and other published manuscripts. Source: Washington University in St. Louis The post Can a vaccine for moms protect infants from a deadly superbug? appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: A teenager built a supply distribution network where families request what they need without filling out any forms or declaring themselves as someone in need. She also added a program that researches each family’s cultural background and sends handmade crafts alongside the package. That’s Vivian Ho, the first nominated Local Changemaker in The Optimist Daily’s new series. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including six countries that just put a dollar figure on their EV investments, a Columbia University finding on the minimum movement needed to offset a desk job, and what pest experts actually recommend instead of vinegar. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hi, everyone. I’m Karissa. Arielle: I’m Arielle. Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. Arielle: So good to be back this week. It’s feeling very spooky over here. How about you, Karissa? Karissa: Super spooky and Halloweeny as we prepare for the holiday over the weekend, and a time change over in the US. I know over in Amsterdam, you’re already having those darker evenings. Arielle: Yes, we had our time change last weekend, and yeah, it does get dark so early, and it feels quite wintry, but that’s all right. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I miss the sun. I know. Maybe a week of this weather and I’ll be longing for the sun, but there is no shortage of good news to brighten your day at The Optimist Daily. Arielle: No, especially because we started publishing our Local Changemakers series this week on Wednesday. You can look forward to one Local Changemaker feature every Wednesday in the run-up to Thanksgiving. This week was a little bit different. We have two features because we have the Student Maker story, which kind of inspired us to highlight younger changemakers this year, and then the first nominated Local Changemaker. Karissa: Mm-hmm. I can’t wait to dive into them. But before we do- Mm … that, we wanna remind you that all these solutions are available in our newsletter format, whether you want that every day or just a weekly digest. It’s free to sign up, and the link to do that is in the show notes. Arielle: If you’re more of a social media feed type of news consumer, then you can follow us on all social platforms, @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are, @OdeToOptimism. You can also reach me and Karissa directly by emailing us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. We really love getting comments, questions, feedback, or anecdotes that you wanna share with us. So yeah, feel free to shoot us an email whenever. Karissa: We also encourage you to share with friends, loved ones, all this positive news from The Optimist Daily, and remind them that, you know, good things are happening out there in the world. As usual, a big thank you to our Emissaries who financially support the mission of The Optimist Daily. If you would like to become an Emissary, the link to do that is also in the show notes. With all of that said and done, shall we jump into the spooky solutions of the week? Let’s get into it. Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician Karissa: The first solution is “Age-by-age Halloween tips from a board-certified pediatrician”. This piece is informed by an actual pediatrician about how to make Halloween work for every kid in your family, and the framing is really specific to each age group in a way that’s genuinely useful. For toddlers, one tip that I thought stood out was to bring a wagon, even if your kid insists they don’t need one when you’re trick-or-treating or attending some kind of Halloween event. For school-aged kids, uh, Dr. Kristen Cook, who is the pediatrician that gives all this advice in the article, frames Halloween as giving earned independence when you’re trick-or-treating, so you can, you know, hang back a couple houses, let the kids lead, but keep them in sight. And then when it comes to teenagers, they might be going to Halloween parties, and at these parties they can come across some peer pressuring situations. It’s good to talk to them about an exit plan for situations they might not be comfortable with and discuss how to deal with these potentially uncomfortable situations, but ultimately trusting them to handle it the right way. So lots of good tips here. This just brings so much Halloween nostalgia back for me. Arielle: Yeah, I, um… my parents didn’t let me participate in Halloween growing up. I know. Heartbreak. I think it just was, uh, you know, we are an immigrant family coming from a very Christian country- Yes, yeah … and they kind of saw it as, like, kind of like devil worship. But, you know, we got over that stage. I was already, um… I kinda aged out of Halloween, uh, in the traditional sense where you go trick-or-treating and all of that. But my youngest sister was able to participate, and she had, like, really fun costumes. As a little kid, she wanted to be a tissue box one year. Um- That’s a good one … which was really weird. It was, like, a High School Musical tissue box, because we had like, High School Musical, um, wrapping paper. And so that’s how she decided to dress up. Karissa: I love it. Arielle: Yeah, so I have vicarious Halloween memories through my youngest sister. Karissa: Well, I mean, as an adult now, maybe you can do some, some of this stuff. NYC food pantries are stocking pet food for struggling households Karissa: The next solution is very heartwarming, and it’s that “New York City food pantries are now stocking pet food for struggling households”. New York State just put $500,000 towards making sure pet owners don’t have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their animals. There are now 22 food pantries across all five boroughs stocking free pet food, and the reason this program exists is kind of heartbreaking and kind of sweet at the same time. The story mentions a woman named Cassandra in Brooklyn who sometimes eats less so her Shih Tzu doesn’t go hungry, and she’s far from alone. The demand for pet food grew after SNAP benefit cuts, which tells you a lot about just how far those cuts reach into people’s lives. Animal welfare groups have known for years that financial hardship and pet surrender are directly linked, but this program is essentially trying to catch families before they hit that wall. 5 research-backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk Karissa: The next solution is a health lifestyle related one, and it’s “Five research backed ways to banish aches and feel better at your desk”. Columbia University researchers ran a study trying to find the minimum effective dose of movement to counteract sitting all day. The answer was actually surprisingly specific. It’s simply five minutes of walking every 30 minutes that makes a difference. NPR actually then tested that with 20,000 of their listeners and found the exact same thing. So this article breaks down that finding plus four other fixes. Arielle, have you ever heard of this tip to walk five minutes every 30 minutes? Arielle: No, but to increase focus, I use the Pomodoro Technique, which is when you set the timer for about 20- 25 minutes and then give yourself a five-minute break. Because I work from home- Yeah … I am always kind of hunched over my laptop. So that is a trick that I use, and I do generally get up and, like, walk around the house. Um- Yeah … so I guess my body intuitively knew that this was a good thing to do, but it’s nice to have the science back it up. Karissa: The whole concept of this kind of, like, movement snack, um, short burst of activity is catching fire and a good suggestion. I guess I’ll mention one more thing about this solution, but you can check out the rest on optimistdaily.com. The whole posture section of this article talks about how the idea of sitting up straight and holding it advice is actually not correct. The actual physical therapist guidance is that your best posture is your next posture, meaning any fixed position causes strain eventually. New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries Karissa: Well, the next solution is “New Jersey Transit is turning commuter stations into art galleries”. NJ Transit has been installing art exhibitions at train and bus stations since 2019, and the program just expanded to its eighth location. The new show is about railroads and 250 years of American history, which is a pretty fun yet informative thing to encounter while you’re just trying to catch your train, the history about railroads. But the whole premise of this is that transit spaces are great for public art because nobody goes there expecting to see any. The encounter is accidental, which makes it different from an intentional gallery visit. I really like this, um, rise of art in public spaces, and it kind of reminds me of a solution we shared a couple months ago about how over in Warsaw they’re putting libraries in commuter stations. So if you have a little time, a layover in transportation, you can go check out the library. So I think this is a really cool kind of global trend. Arielle: And it’s really nice that the program actually pays the artists stipends because public art rarely comes with a real budget, and a lot of the time public art is like a, a mural that maybe someone painted for free or graffiti, which honestly, I’m a huge fan of graffiti. Some of the tags are really impressive, and some of them- Yeah … are just kind of silly, but they’re entertaining in their own way. Um, but that obviously doesn’t come with payment. If anything, it might come with a fine. Karissa: Right. Exactly. In this broader conversation about what public spaces are for, whether that’s a transit station, a library, park, you know, it can be a lot more than just something that people move through. Student Makers: bringing free STEM to students on three continents Karissa: Moving on to the Changemaker series, we talked more about Student Makers in this deeper dive. They are a group bringing free STEM to students on three continents. And like Arielle mentioned, this is the story that made us decide to make the entire series this year about people under 30, because young people are really just doing so many impressive things to change the world. At Student Makers, former students become the instructors. It’s often high schoolers teaching middle schoolers, and the founder’s whole argument is that it’s more relatable to have, um, you know, people who are closer in age to you to help teach things than an adult expert teaching the same material. Like we mentioned, we’ll have some of the main players behind Student Makers on the podcast in the beginning of 2027, which is crazy to even say that 2027 is around the corner. But we look forward to welcoming them on and hearing directly from them. Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity Arielle: I will take over from here, Karissa, and my first solution is actually the first nominated changemaker for this series. The title- Ooh … of the article is “Meet Vivian Ho, the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity”. Most programs that distribute supplies to low-income families ask that family to identify themselves before they get anything. So basically, you have to fill out a form, you check a box, you explain your situation to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built her nonprofit, All the Same organization, around removing that whole process. Families request what they need anonymously, and nobody has to declare themselves as someone in need to get the help they need. And she started this at just 16, which is quite impressive. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: The anonymous sign-up system is what makes this really special. Vivian’s read on situations like this was that the stigma of asking for help was keeping families from asking at all. So she just said, “Let’s get rid of that.” There’s also something within this nonprofit. There’s another, uh, initiative called the Cultural Surprises program, and it’s something I hadn’t seen before. So volunteers research the cultural background of the family they’re packing for, and handmade crafts reflecting that culture go out alongside the supply package, and it turns a resource delivery into something more like recognition, something that makes that family feel really seen. I’m not gonna get into all of the details, but I do encourage people who are interested in learning more about Vivian Ho and perhaps how to support her work to check out the article because it is really, really remarkable that she was able to do this as a teenager. Karissa: Congratulations to Vivian for being nominated by two of The Optimist Daily community members who are involved with the project as well, a nomination from her co-founder and a volunteer that she inspired to start his own project nominated Vivian. So go check that out if you wanna learn more. Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems Arielle: The next solution is titled “Kenya unlocks $160 million to protect the Maasai Mara and Tsavo ecosystems”. Kenya just signed a $160 million deal to protect nearly 67,000 square miles of some of the most important wildlife habitat in Africa, including the Maasai Mara and Tsavo. But the interesting part isn’t just the money, it’s the structure of how that money gets released, because this isn’t a grant that arrives and then disappears. So the funding mechanism is called Project Finance for Permanence. Money flows in tied to specific government policy benchmarks, and not all the money gets, uh, given upfront, let’s say. If Kenya doesn’t hit the milestones, then those funds never get released. Tsavo holds 40% of Kenya’s elephants and 20% of its critically endangered black rhinos, and that’s just to give you an idea of what’s at stake for wildlife and geographically. Kenya committed to the global 30 by 30 target and was sitting at about 20% to 23% coverage, so this deal would largely close that gap by 2030. Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works Arielle: The next solution is titled, “Will vinegar actually keep bugs out this fall? Pest experts explain what works.” So every fall, people reach for the vinegar bottle as a first line of pest defense. They spray the windows, they spray the door frames, and then it feels like they’ve done something. But two pest control experts basically say, “You’ve done nothing.” The reason why is in this article, and there’s also one fall tip in here that’s actually kind of strange and useful. So vinegar unfortunately only kills soft-bodied insects on direct wet contact, and then once it dries, then the vinegar doesn’t really do anything against cockroaches, beetles, spiders, or ants. And researchers found negligible effects on most common household insects. What really works is, like, caulking windows and weather-stripping doors and adding door sweeps. That will actually stop bugs from getting in. Spraying is just treating the symptom and not really addressing the entry point of where all of these pests try to come in and get cozy ’cause the weather outside is getting worse. Um- Yeah … and then the, the weird tip, well, I found it weird or unexpected, is the acorn tip. If you are bringing acorns or pine cones inside this fall, then you should put them in 150-degree Fahrenheit oven for about 30 minutes first, and that will kill whatever’s living inside them, and then you can, like, decorate your home for the holidays in peace knowing that there’s no hidden critter in your pine cone just waiting to make your house their home. Karissa: Exactly. Arielle: The DIY home pest control has surged since the pandemic. People want low-chemical solutions, and that’s why I think vinegar gets so much reach. But yeah, unfortunately it’s just not as effective as everyone thought it was. Karissa: Well, it’s good to know so we don’t waste our vinegar and our time. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Yeah. Karissa: I- I have to say, though, maybe this is bad, but I do like to use just the harsh chemicals and get them out of the way- … if they do come in the house. So I, I don’t hesitate to use the big stuff. Arielle: Yeah. It’s… You know, we appreciate your honesty here. I’m sure there are a lot of listeners who struggle with pests and are like, “Yeah, I’m just gonna obliterate.” The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs Arielle: The next solution is titled, “The seven best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs”. Grocery prices are unfortunately still high, and two university horticulture experts say there are specific vegetables that genuinely pay for themselves when you grow them at home. Most of the list made sense to me, but there’s one of them that takes three years before it really starts producing, and both experts say plant it anyway. And yeah, there are pretty good reasons, which I will get into. So first, herbs are the economic winner here. They’re among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store. You usually buy more than you use, and growing them means you harvest exactly what you need when you need it. The strange one was the asparagus. It takes two to three years of establishment before you get a real harvest, so you really have to be committed to the asparagus, and also you have to like asparagus. I like asparagus, but I know a lot of people aren’t the biggest fans. But a well-maintained bed produces for up to 20 years. One expert calls it something you’ll have basically for life. Both experts are clear that the garden only saves money if you plant what your household actually eats. So start with vegetables you already go through the most, and that will help you save money in the end. How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility Arielle: The last solution that we are gonna share with everyone this week is titled “How EV fleets are shielding Europe from oil price volatility”. So there is that conflict in Iran that has been driving oil prices up 33% this year. But six European countries collectively avoided nearly $2.2 billion in oil import costs just because they have enough EVs on the road. That’s not a projection or a goal, that’s an actual number from a six-month window. Denmark alone displaced 13% of its entire 2025 oil consumption. So there’s a real dollar security argument for EV adoption here that goes beyond anything to do with the environment, although the environment is very important. Karissa: Yes. Arielle: Hopefully this, uh, this will encourage other economies to really invest in their EV development, but also hopefully this conflict ends soon. Karissa: Yeah. So- For multiple reasons, of course. But it just goes to show how moving towards renewable energy, sustainable energy across the board is just the best path towards energy security. Arielle: Definitely. Well, those were all of the solutions we had this week, but before we go, we have a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “Part of being optimistic is keeping one’s head pointed toward the sun, one’s feet moving forward.” And that’s from Nelson Mandela. Arielle: Beautiful. Well, everyone, I hope you enjoy your Halloween weekend if you’re celebrating, and if not, then I hope you enjoy the, uh, candy sales that are inevitably- going to happen after Halloween is over. We will both be back next week with more solutions. Karissa: Until then, have a great weekend. The post Podcast Transcript October 30th, 2026— Kenya’s wildlife deal, Halloween tips across the ages, and EV energy security first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: Στην Dorothy, μια τρανς ηθοποιός, η Jeeva έχει περάσει μεγάλο μέρος του ταξιδιού της πλοηγώντας σε μια πραγματικότητα όπου η ταυτότητά της μπορεί να επισκιάσει το ταλέντο της. Ευκαιρίες που πρέπει να καταλήγουν σε δεξιότητες και πάθος συχνά γίνονται μάχες ενάντια στην προκατάληψη. Αλλά δεν θέλει να τη γιορτάζουν μόνο για το σπάσιμο των φραγμών. Θέλει να την αναγνωρίζουν για τις ερμηνείες της, αυτή…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Dorothy a transgender actor, Jeeva has spent much of her journey navigating a reality where her identity can overshadow her talent. Opportunities that should come down to skill and passion often become battles against prejudice. But she doesn't want to be celebrated only for breaking barriers. She wants to be recognised for her performances, her craft and the stories she brings to life on screen. Her journey brings attention to a larger issue in Indian cinema: transgender artists deserve more than occasional representation. They deserve equal opportunities, meaningful roles and the freedom to build careers without constantly having to prove they belong. Because representation isn't just about being seen. It's about being given the chance to shine. Έχει επίσης ζήσει με διπολική διαταραχή για πάνω από δύο δεκαετίες. Εδώ, μοιράζεται τις επτά «θεραπείες» - από την αγάπη της οικογένειάς της μέχρι μια ρουτίνα ύπνου που αποκαλεί «θρησκεία» - που τη βοηθούν…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article has been published in partnership with India Mental Health Alliance. Aparna Piramal Raje is a writer, columnist, bestselling author, and mother of two. She has also lived with bipolar disorder for over two decades. Here, she shares the seven 'therapies' — from her family's love to a sleep routine she calls 'religion' — that help her live a full, happy life. It is March 2013, and I am at a yoga ashram in Bihar for a weeklong retreat. And I am coming apart. I haven't slept more than three hours a night in several days. I'm talking to myself. There are voices in my head, and my thoughts are so scattered and disorganised that I can't hold on to any of them. I am having a psychotic breakdown. When the retreat ends, I can't manage the journey back to Mumbai on my own. My husband has to come and get me, and escort me home. Aparna beside a poster for a 2022 talk about her book and her mental health journey. Seeing the state I'm in, I'm taken to a psychiatrist and put on medication. And for the first time, what I have been living with gets a name: bipolar disorder, a serious mental health condition. Thirteen years without a name The diagnosis was new. The condition was not. It had first surfaced in the year 2000, when I was in my mid-20s, and remained undiagnosed for more than a decade. I had been raised in Mumbai and London and studied at Harvard Business School and Oxford University. I had worked in my family's office furniture business and as a journalist. Through all of it, I had been riding highs and lows I didn't understand. Aparna pictured horse riding with her sister, who remains one of her closest sources of support. Looking back, I can see the pattern. Too many projects and deadlines pushed me into mania more than once, in both jobs. Work, for me, had become a trigger. After the ashram, I recovered from the psychosis, only to be plunged into depression for several months. Eventually, I came out of that too. " I don't consider myself unwell, even though it is an illness" It may sound strange, but the diagnosis came as a relief. For the first time, my family and I had a roadmap for how to treat and manage what was happening to me. Aparna began studying at Harvard Business School in 2000, the year her symptoms first surfaced. It also taught me what bipolar disorder actually is. As I understand it, it is a mood disorder brought on by psychological triggers and chemical imbalances in the brain. It causes extreme shifts in mood. At one end is mania: energetic phases where I barely sleep, have delusions of grandeur, and sometimes tip into psychosis. At the other end is depression, when I am low on energy and in low spirits. In between, there are long stretches of stability and normalcy, though every patient's cycles are different. Aparna with her sister Radhika in their 20s; she later described her sister as a key support. Everyone has mood swings, so please don't assume you are bipolar because you have some. Bipolar disorder means extreme swings, and very specific changes in behaviour. Most importantly, the diagnosis showed me that personality and illness are different things. I have a normal personality. I also have a medical condition that needs to be managed and treated, like any other medical condition. Aparna photographed in Laax in March 2018, during a manic episode, five years after her bipolar disorder diagnosis. So I don't consider myself unwell, even though it is an illness. That insight became the bedrock of my self-acceptance — and without self-acceptance, no healing can take place. Learning to survive I'm an optimist by nature, and I always look for solutions. Over the next ten years, it was these solutions and "hacks" that helped me heal and recover. It took a lot to make everything come together: the right medication, a trustworthy doctor, supportive family and friends, a manageable job, a spiritual practice, self-reflection, and fulfilling lifestyle pursuits. At times, it felt like a matter of tremendous planetary alignment! Aparna at the 2015 launch of Working Out of the Box, which preceded Chemical Khichdi. But I came to see that three "therapies" are essential just to survive, especially in a crisis. None of them can be substituted. The first is medical therapy. I see my psychiatrist, take additional medication when I need it, and continue talk therapy. I cannot stress enough how much a good therapist matters. As I understand it, my mood episodes are psychological triggers causing chemical imbalances. If I haven't slept well for five nights in a row, I'm likely to tip into hypomania. But what is keeping me awake for five nights in a row? That is usually something psychological. Aparna with her husband Amit, whom she credits as a key part of her support system. Therapy helps me find those triggers, understand myself, and manage my mood swings. I've seen therapists for two decades, and they've given me incredible insight into what lies beneath my ups and downs. I still see mine every fortnight. It is essential to my stability. The second is love therapy — the care of the people closest to me. For me, that is my husband, my two sons and my sister. All of them look after me when I'm unwell, and I'm lucky to have their unconditional support and acceptance. Aparna with relatives at a family gathering; she says family support is central to her recovery. The third is lifestyle therapy. Self-care turned out to be just as necessary as doctors and caregivers. A disciplined lifestyle matters for everyone, but especially for those of us living with a mental health challenge. I exercise regularly, play games, and eat a nutritious diet. But sleep, as far as I'm concerned, is religion. A regular sleep routine is the single biggest factor in my emotional and mental well-being, and I'm much happier now that I'm disciplined about it. Aparna with friends; she describes trusted relationships as important to managing her health. So I have dinner at home with my husband and kids most evenings. I rarely go out at night more than twice a week, and I don't work after dinner. Most nights, I get my seven to eight hours. Learning to thrive Surviving is one thing. Thriving — being well enough to write a book, or to stand before strangers and talk about my mental health — needed something more. It needed self-reflection, self-inquiry and inner work. That is where the other four therapies came in. Self-therapy began on the page. I journal, I use positive affirmations, and I keep returning to both to understand what triggers my mood swings and how to regulate my emotions. Aparna visited her Oxford college in 2025; she studied at Oxford before her 2013 diagnosis. Spiritual therapy came through a regular study of Vedanta. It helped me look at the root causes of my ups and downs, and it has made me calmer and more at peace. The therapy of empathy came from other people. Mental health, I've learnt, is a team sport, so I made a point of asking for help. I shared my vulnerability with many friends, mentors and colleagues, and it made a huge difference. Aparna at a panel discussion for Working Out of the Box, published before Chemical Khichdi. These allies made safe spaces for me to share my thoughts and emotions, during manic or depressive phases and in recovery afterwards. They turned listening into an art form. They offered acceptance, patience, empathy and advice without judgement — and sometimes stepped in directly when things got difficult. If it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a community of allies to heal a mind. Aparna's book 'Chemical Khichdi' chronicles her journey of living with bipolar disorder and recovery. Work therapy was the one I least expected. Work had pushed me into mania before, so how could it ever be therapeutic? Over time, I learnt that structured, fulfilling work could be an anchor. Approached with the right balance and intention, it gives me stability and meaning, along with a sense of control, accomplishment and identity. It is no longer only about income or career. It is a way to channel my energy constructively, and to build the routines that help me manage my moods. Aparna at an event marking her first independent board appointment during her working life. The strategy that makes this possible is what I call playing 'opposite-handed'. Imagine playing a sport with your other hand: you'd play more mindfully and more slowly. That's how I now work. I recognise my limits and take breaks before I burn out, and this has let me thrive at work despite how unpredictable bipolar disorder can be. Aparna teaching a group of students; she describes fulfilling work as a source of stability. Together, these four therapies helped me understand myself, regulate myself, and move from just coping to thriving. Back on the stage By May 2022, I had been stable for over four years. That month, I stood on stage at the Royal Opera House in Mumbai, one of India's most prestigious theatres, in front of 400 people. I made a speech, and my sister and I released my book, Chemical Khichdi: How I Hacked My Mental Health — the story of my journey of healing and recovery. Aparna at the launch of Chemical Khichdi, her 2022 book about her mental health journey. It went on to become an official national bestseller. Over the next few years, I was invited to speak at 150 talks across the country and online, breaking taboos about mental health. Then, in November 2025, I stood on a stage in Bangalore among eleven brave women, each of us holding a copy of Homecoming: Mental Health Journeys of Resilience, Healing and Wholeness. Written by Neha Kirpal and Dr Nandini Murali, it is a unique anthology of Indian women's mental health journeys, and mine is one of them. Aparna with other women at a 2025 event for Homecoming, an anthology of mental health journeys. A few years earlier, Neha and I had talked about her hopes of writing a book. Now Chemical Khichdi was being seen as a forerunner in a growing movement of mental health books in India, and I was beginning to be seen as a mental health advocate. It was deeply satisfying. Happy, thriving and bipolar Today, I'm 50. I live in Mumbai with my husband, our two teenage sons and my in-laws, and I work as a writer, columnist and public speaker. In more than two decades of living with bipolar disorder, I've had about a dozen episodes of mania, or its milder form, hypomania. That's quite a lot. But I haven't had a full-blown manic episode or depression in over eight years, and I have a "normal" personal and professional life. Aparna at a Chemical Khichdi launch event; the book later became a national bestseller. The mood swings haven't vanished. I still feel things with more intensity and volatility than most people. The difference is that I'm in control now (well, most of the time). I've learnt to witness my emotions without being consumed by them, using these seven therapies. I believe happiness is a decision. For me, it is a choice and a daily practice, and these therapies are my everyday toolkit. Aparna signing copies of Chemical Khichdi, which led to invitations to speak across India. I have also come to realise that my vulnerability is my guru. My bipolarity has been my biggest source of illumination. Nearly ten years ago, I wrote this in my journal: "I have come to realise that the stronger you are, the more hurt you can handle. And the less you share that hurt with anyone, the more the accumulated emotion. I've experienced every possible negative emotion - anger, frustration, resentment, fear and paranoia. It has made me volatile, manic, uncontrollable, deluded, sleep-deprived and generally a pain to handle. Aparna at a book club gathering; she continues to work as a writer, columnist and speaker. But from that has emerged so much that's good about my life: truth, compassion, wisdom, patience and most of all, love. Could I live without being bipolar? Absolutely. And my family would echo that ten times over. But it has provided me the opportunity to examine my life like no other." If you're where I once was I've come a long way since that ashram in 2013. So here is what I'd want you to know. There's no need to be scared of a mental health condition. In my experience, it can be managed like any physical health condition. Recognise the symptoms early, and respond before things escalate. It's difficult at first, but it gets much easier with time, and it doesn't have to stand in the way of a family life, a social life or a career. Aparna speaking about Chemical Khichdi; she has delivered talks on mental health across India. Take charge of your mental health. Get timely professional advice. Tell your family what's going on, and accept their help. Rest and slow down when you need to. Make allies, and open up to them. And develop your own therapies and hacks. Whether you live with bipolar disorder or any other mental health condition, I hope my story encourages you to get help when you need it. You can live the life you want to.

Σε όλη την Ινδία,…
items.descriptionOriginal: After sugarcane is crushed for its juice, a fibrous residue called bagasse is left behind. At sugar mills, heaps of this material can be seen awaiting their next use. While some bagasse is already used to generate energy or make paper, it also holds potential for products that can replace plastic — and even become a source of protein. Across India, entrepreneurs and young innovators are exploring these possibilities. From compostable plates and takeaway boxes to fermentation-based protein, here are four ventures finding new value in sugarcane waste. 1. Chuk: Turning sugarcane fibre into compostable tableware When Ved Krishna returned to his family's paper business in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, he began questioning the environmental cost of conventional food packaging. Plastic-coated and laminated materials were widely used, yet their disposal posed a growing problem. In 2017, his family's company, Pakka Limited, launched Chuk to offer an alternative. The brand uses bagasse, the fibrous residue left after sugarcane juice extraction, to manufacture plates, bowls, food containers and other tableware. The fibre is processed into pulp, which is then moulded into finished products. The resulting tableware is designed to be sturdy enough for everyday food service while offering an alternative to conventional plastic and Styrofoam disposables. Ved Krishna's Chuk uses sugarcane bagasse to make compostable plates, bowls and food containers for everyday food service. Photograph: ( TRASH ) Chuk's products are used by food and hospitality businesses, including Haldiram's, Starbucks and Chai Point. According to the company's earlier reporting, its tableware can decompose within approximately 60 days under suitable conditions. By giving sugarcane residue a second life, Chuk demonstrates how an agricultural byproduct can become a practical replacement for disposable plastic products. 3. Ecoware: Packaging that can return to the soil After witnessing the scale of plastic pollution in India, Rhea Mazumdar Singhal left her pharmaceutical career in the UK to work on an alternative to single-use packaging. She founded Ecoware in 2010, building a business around plant-based food-service products. Sugarcane bagasse is among the principal materials used in its range of plates, bowls, trays and takeaway containers. The fibre is converted into pulp and shaped under high heat and pressure using precision moulds. Ecoware says its products contain no plastic lining, adhesive, laminate or coating, allowing the material to break down naturally under suitable conditions. Founded by Rhea Mazumdar Singhal, Ecoware turns plant-based materials, including sugarcane fibre, into alternatives to single-use plastic packaging. Photograph: ( Lifestyle Asia ) The company reports that its products can biodegrade in soil in around 100 days in the presence of microbes. Its range is designed for practical food-service needs, including serving hot meals and packing takeaway orders. Ecoware's approach addresses two problems at once : the accumulation of disposable plastic and the underuse of agricultural residue. By offering businesses and households a plant-based alternative, it helps make lower-waste food packaging a more accessible everyday choice. 3. Dinearth: Making sustainable food packaging more accessible Dinearth, a sustainable packaging initiative founded by Harsh and Jani, backed by Abhinav Industries, brings bagasse-based alternatives to the food-service sector. The business draws on its parent company's experience in food packaging to offer products designed for restaurants, takeaway counters and catering businesses. Its manufacturing process begins with sugarcane bagasse sourced from sugar mills. The residue is converted into pulp and pressed into moulds using heat and pressure to create disposable food packaging. Its catalogue includes plates, trays, bowls and takeaway boxes, offering businesses alternatives to plastic and Styrofoam containers. Dinearth's EcoDine range offers bagasse-based plates, bowls and takeaway boxes, with select products reportedly priced from around Re 1 per unit. Photograph: ( Otarapack ) An important part of this approach is making the switch practical for smaller food vendors, not just large restaurant chains. Dinearth's EcoDine range has been presented as a more affordable line of biodegradable tableware, with reported prices starting at around Rs1 per unit for select products. By combining familiar food-service formats with plant-fibre materials, Dinearth seeks to make alternatives to conventional disposables easier to adopt across a wider range of businesses. 4. Kinva Bio: Exploring sugarcane waste as a source of protein What if agricultural residue could help meet the demand for protein? That is the question behind Kinva Bio, a venture developed by students Nitish and Gulshan Kumar at the National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management in Haryana. Instead of turning bagasse into a disposable product, the team is exploring how fungal fermentation can convert agricultural byproducts into mycoprotein, a protein-rich material produced using fungi. Sugarcane bagasse serves as one of the potential feedstocks. By giving agricultural residue a new purpose, Indian innovators are exploring alternatives to plastic disposables and new uses for biomass. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The process combines biotechnology with artificial intelligence. Fungal fermentation converts the biomass, while an AI-powered digital twin helps predict protein yields and optimise production conditions. The aim is to develop a way of producing protein that could require less land and water than conventional sources. Kinva Bio remains an emerging innovation rather than an established, large-scale food producer. Its work nevertheless points to another possibility for agricultural waste: using biotechnology to turn low-value residue into a potential food resource. Sources: 'Ayodhya-based CHUK is turning sugarcane waste into sustainable cutlery for Indian Railways, Google, Amazon' by Rashi Varshney for YourStory, Published on 30 December 2020. EcoWare Dinearth 'From Sonipat to the Future of Food: Two Young Innovators Turn Crop Waste into Sustainable Protein' by samsung Newsroom India, Published on 18 October 2026

items.description: Τα τρόφιμα ευθύνονται για το ένα τρίτο των εκπομπών του θερμοκηπίου της ανθρωπότητας. Και σίγουρα, τα τρόφιμα που εκπέμπουν περισσότερο άνθρακα είναι επίσης αυτά που τείνουν να είναι τα χειρότερα για την υγεία μας, όπως τα κρέατα και τα γαλακτοκομικά. items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine
